en: The Sutra of the Great Dharma-Collection Asked by Mahākāśyapa, Spoken by the Buddha,
Scroll One.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Chao San Da Fu, Acting Assistant Director of the Court of State Ceremonial.
Translated by the Dharma-transmitting Master, the Subject Shi Hu, by imperial decree: Thus have I heard:

At one time the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of eight thousand bhikṣus and sixteen thousand bodhisattvas, as well as those who had attained supreme, perfect, and complete enlightenment in their final birth, all of whom had gathered from various buddha-fields.
At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa was sitting serenely amidst the great assembly.
Then the World-Honored One addressed Kāśyapa, saying:
"There are four kinds of dharmas that destroy the wisdom of a bodhisattva."
Kāśyapa replied, “What is the meaning of these four kinds of dharmas? [The Buddha said:
“The four kinds of dharmas are:”
First, to give rise to contempt for the Buddha’s teachings;
second, to harbor hatred and jealousy toward Dharma teachers;
third, to conceal the true Dharma so that it is neither seen nor heard.

Fourth, they repeatedly obstruct others who desire the Dharma; out of malice, they sever roots of goodness and conceal them from being spoken; they deceive others while seeking only their own profit. Kāśyapa!
These four kinds are called the destruction of a bodhisattva’s wisdom.
Regarding this, I shall now speak again in verse:
“If a person is arrogant toward the Buddha-dharma;”
Hating and envying the Dharma teacher;
delighting in the Dharma yet concealing it;
being wrathful and severing the roots of goodness; covering up the Dharma and not preaching it.
Delighting in deceiving others, and constantly acting to seek one's own profit—
I say that these four dharmas sever the wisdom of a bodhisattva.
Because these four dharmas are thus, you all should know them.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"There are four supreme contemplations of the Dharma that increase the great wisdom of a bodhisattva.
Kāśyapa addressed him, saying:
"What is the meaning of this? "These four dharmas are:
first, to engender profound respect for the Buddha’s teachings;..."
Second, do not give rise to contempt or arrogance toward the Dharma teacher;
third, having received the Dharma as you have heard it, explain it for others while giving rise to an upright mind and seeking no gain or honor whatsoever;
fourth, praise extensive learning which increases wisdom, maintain a single-mindedly correct mind to receive and uphold the teachings as heard, and practice true conduct without speaking falsely.
Kāśyapa! These four dharmas cause the great wisdom of a bodhisattva to increase.
Now, regarding this, I shall speak again in verse:
"Revering the Buddha's Dharma, as well as the place where the Dharma teacher dwells;
explaining it to others just as one has heard it, without seeking gain or offerings, nor desiring praise, but seeking only to hear."
Much learning gives rise to wisdom; as one has heard, so one receives and upholds the Dharma.
Having upheld it, one practices according to the Dharma, for it accords with the reality of the Dharma.
This is the practice of that Dharma-master: his speech and mind are free from falsehood.
"Four dharmas can serve as teachers, leading one to attain the great wisdom of a Buddha.
The Buddha told Mahākāśyapa:
"There are four dharmas, when fully possessed, that obscure and obstruct the bodhicitta of a bodhisattva."
Kāśyapa replied, “What are the four dharmas that delude and obstruct the bodhicitta?
“These four dharmas are:”
First, to give rise to slander against one's own ācārya teachers and all virtuous friends whose conduct and virtue are worthy of respect;
second, to destroy the flourishing virtues of others;
third, when sentient beings practice the Mahāyāna path, not to praise them but instead to speak falsely and slanderously.
Fourth, to reject and turn one's back on the correct mind while engaging in false and deluded discrimination. Thus, Kāśyapa,
these four kinds of dharmas delude and obstruct the bodhicitta of a bodhisattva.
I shall now speak again in verse regarding this matter:
"The preceptor, the teacher, and the virtuous friend— In conduct and virtue, all are worthy of respect;
Yet failing to cultivate a heart of reverence, One instead gives rise to contempt and disparagement."
His own virtue increases and blazes intensely, yet he destroys and eliminates others;
this practitioner of the Great Way to Bodhi slanders and treats with contempt those who practice it;
turning his back on the true mind, he discriminates through false delusions.
These four types of evil conduct Obscure and obstruct the Buddha’s bodhi.
Therefore, these four dharmas Keep one far from unsurpassed awakening;
One who is free from these four faults Attains the supreme bodhi.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:

"If four qualities are fully possessed, they cause all bodhisattvas to give rise to the bodhicitta in every place of birth, proceeding directly until they sit at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) without any hindrance."
Kāśyapa replied, "What are the four dharmas? [The Buddha said:
"First, not to engage in wrong views, false speech, or frivolous talk for the sake of one's own body or life."
Second, to eliminate all false conceptualizations of all sentient beings;
third, to act as the Buddha’s messenger to initiate all the signs of the seeds of bodhi, so that their true names spread throughout the four quarters;
fourth, to teach and transform all sentient beings so that they attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, each proclaiming, "I have now attained it."

Kāśyapa! A bodhisattva who is fully endowed with these four dharmas gives rise to the bodhicitta in every place of birth, remains free from delusion throughout, and proceeds directly until sitting upon the seat of enlightenment at the site of awakening.
I shall now speak again in verse on this matter:
"For the sake of one's own body or life, One should not engage in false teachings or lying;
With a mind that always has compassion for sentient beings, One should eliminate delusion and indolence."
Able to act as the Tathāgata’s messenger and serve as the teacher of sentient beings,
manifesting the practice of awakening, their fame shall spread throughout the four quarters.
They shall transform all sentient beings, causing them to achieve unsurpassed enlightenment.
Abiding within this Dharma, the bodhicitta shall not regress.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
“There are four dharmas, when fully possessed, which cause all wholesome dharmas—both those already arisen and those yet to arise—in the bodhisattvas to be extinguished and never again to increase.”
Kāśyapa replied, “What are these four dharmas? [The Buddha said:
“First, being deeply attached to the view of self regarding all that exists in the world;”
Second, observing the lineage and dwelling in attachment while performing acts of mantra-power for the sake of gain;
third, harboring resentment toward bodhisattvas and praising the Buddha’s teachings in a biased manner rather than universally extolling them;
fourth, hearing sutras and dharmas that have not been heard before or are difficult to perceive, and then doubting or slandering them.
Thus it is, Kāśyapa!
Possessing these four dharmas causes all wholesome dharmas—both those already arisen and those yet to arise—in Bodhisattvas to be utterly extinguished and never again to increase.
Regarding this, I shall now speak again in verse:
"By this attachment to the view of self, all wholesome dharmas are exhausted;
they scrutinize one's lineage and seek gain through incantations;
they disparage the Bodhisattva teachings and do not universally praise them."
Not having heard profound sutras, they hear them and give rise to doubt and slander;
possessing these four practices, their wholesome dharmas will soon be exhausted.
Therefore, all bodhisattvas who practice these four dharmas [should avoid them].
"They will be far removed from the Buddha’s bodhi, like heaven and earth.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"If four qualities are fully possessed, they cause the wholesome dharmas of all bodhisattvas not to perish, and they cause those dharmas to increase and become superior."
Kāśyapa replied, “What are the four dharmas? [The Buddha said:
“First, one desires to hear of their virtues and not their faults; one seeks to practice the six pāramitās and the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.”
Second, by eliminating the view of self and practicing equanimity, they cause all sentient beings to obtain the benefit of the Dharma and rejoice;

third, by remaining far removed from wrong livelihood, they attain the joy of the noble lineage, refraining from speaking of the real or unreal faults of others and not perceiving the transgressions of others;

fourth, even if this profound Dharma is not seen through their own wisdom, they do not slander or disparage those Buddhas and Tathāgatas, but see it thus and know it thus, thinking: "I cannot know the Buddha’s wisdom, which is boundless, manifold, and unimpeded; the Tathāgata has expounded this Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings."
In this way, Kāśyapa!
By possessing these four dharmas, the wholesome dharmas of all bodhisattvas shall not be exhausted, and they will attain the further increase and excellence of those dharmas.
Now, regarding this, I shall speak again in verse:
"May I always wish to hear of their virtues, And never wish to hear of their evils;
Constantly practicing the six pāramitās, I seek the Bodhisattva-piṭaka;
Severing the view of self, I practice a mind of equanimity."
May all sentient beings universally obtain the joy of those dharma-benefits;
may they live by a pure livelihood and further encounter the noble lineage.
Regarding the faults of others, whether real or unreal, one shall never speak of them.
Even if one should behold various transgressions, One should regard them as if never seen or heard;
This Dharma is most profound and subtle, Such that those of little wisdom cannot know it.
Only the Buddha understands it clearly by himself, And thus gives rise to neither doubt nor slander.
The Buddha’s wisdom is vast and boundless; the Tathāgata has taught it for the sake of the multitudes.
Those who practice these four dharmas will possess inexhaustible, supreme wisdom.
Abiding within these dharmas, awakening is not difficult to attain.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"There are four kinds of dharmas that give rise to improper thoughts and cause one to deviate from the bodhisattva practice.
Kāśyapa addressed him, saying:
"What are the four dharmas?
First, harboring doubt regarding the Buddha's teachings and lacking a heart of devotion;
second, being arrogant due to the view of self and feeling anger toward sentient beings."
Third, coveting the gains and offerings obtained by others, and feeling hatred and envy;
fourth, failing to give rise to faith and respect for the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, neither praising them nor even refraining from slandering them.
Kāśyapa! These four dharmas give rise to an improper mind and cause one to depart from the practice of a bodhisattva.
Regarding this, I shall now speak again in verse:
They harbor doubts regarding the various Buddha-dharmas, And with deliberate intent, they find no joy in them;
Their arrogance and view of self increase, Because they feel hatred toward sentient beings;
When others obtain gain and offerings, They give rise to greed, attachment, and jealous resentment.
"Regarding the Buddha, the Bodhisattvas, and the assembly, they do not give rise to faith or acceptance in their hearts.
These four types of improper mental states keep one far removed from the bodhisattva practice.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
“There are four kinds of dharmas that cause bodhisattvas to attain the mark of suppleness.
Kāśyapa said: “What are these four dharmas?”

"First, regarding the *abhrānti* (non-delusion) one has attained: having attained it, one confesses it and never conceals it, thereby remaining far removed from faults. Second, one must be true to reality and sincere in speech;

even if it means exhausting one's royal status, destroying wealth and honor, dispersing profits, or sacrificing one's own life, one shall never speak falsely. One’s words must be truthful, and one shall not cause others to speak what is false.

Third, one shall not utter evil words to slander or despise any sentient being. Even regarding matters such as good and evil, quarreling, striking, or binding with shackles and fetters—one shall not speak of such transgressions, for fear of personally incurring sin and receiving the retribution of karma."
Fourth, based on that practice of faith, they have deep faith in all the Buddha’s teachings and their minds are pure. Kāśyapa!
These four dharmas cause bodhisattvas to attain the mark of suppleness.
I now speak again in verse regarding this matter:
"The *āpatti* I have incurred, fearing it may become a transgression, I dare not conceal it myself;
with a purified mind, I confess and reveal it."
One's intentions must be sincere, and what one says must be truthful;
rather than exhausting the rank of a king, or sacrificing life and wealth,
one must not utter false speech nor abandon the practice of truth.
Nor does one instruct others to engage in false or deceptive acts;
nor does one practice slander or hold in contempt any group of beings,
whether virtuous or non-virtuous, including those involved in strife and contention.
Never speak of others, for fear of inviting the fruits of one’s own karma;
let the mind abide in pure conduct and take faith and joy in the Buddha’s Bodhi.
These four things the Buddhas proclaim—sentient beings should draw near to them.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"There are four kinds of dharmas that cause the minds of bodhisattvas to become rigid and stubborn.
Kāśyapa addressed him, saying:
“What are the four dharmas?
First, not delighting in practicing the most supreme and excellent Dharma one has heard;
second, although knowing the distinction between what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma, as well as purity and defilement, one does not practice pure Dharma but instead practices non-Dharma.”
Third, they do not draw near to ācāryas or teachers of the Dharma, and having accepted false speech with faith, they do not know the proper measure of food;
fourth, when seeing bodhisattvas endowed with supreme virtues, they lack all reverence and instead treat them with arrogance and contempt due to their view of self.
Kāśyapa! These four dharmas cause the minds and intentions of bodhisattvas to become rigid and stubborn.
Regarding this, I shall now speak again in verse:
"Having heard that supreme Dharma, their minds find no joy in practicing it;
they do not cultivate the pure Dharma, but instead develop a fondness for what is contrary to the Dharma;
they turn their backs on the ācārya and show no reverence for the Teacher’s Dharma."
Not knowing the proper place for receiving food, they practice speech of falsehood;
though the Bodhisattva possesses supreme virtues, they fail to give rise to respect;
their inferior view of self increases, and with hearts of stubbornness, they are full of contempt.
"These four were proclaimed by the Buddhas themselves; I, too, always remain far removed from them.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"There are four kinds of dharmas that cause a bodhisattva’s knowledge and vision to become clear and lucid."
Kāśyapa replied, "What are the four dharmas? [The Buddha said:

"First, one delights in practicing what is heard that is good and delights in ceasing from what is heard that is evil; knowing the reality of the Dharma, one rejects the false and deviant and accepts and practices the right path."
Second, being free from slander and endowed with pure goodness, one’s elegant speech circulates widely and is loved and respected by all;
third, drawing near to the teacher’s instruction and knowing the proper place for sustenance, one subdues the sense faculties and maintains uninterrupted discipline and meditative concentration;
fourth, having attained enlightenment oneself, one does not abandon sentient beings, practicing true compassion to cause them to love and delight in vast and genuine virtues.
Kāśyapa! These four dharmas cause a bodhisattva’s knowledge and vision to become clear and lucid.
Regarding this, I shall now speak again in verse:
Hearing what is good, one desires to practice it; hearing what is evil, one desires to cease from it.
Abandoning false and deceptive causes, one accepts and practices the Eightfold Noble Path;
always remaining far removed from slander, one attains correspondence with wholesome karma.
He spreads forth the sound of virtuous speech, causing sentient beings to cherish and revere it;
he draws near to the teacher’s instruction and knows the source from which their food comes;
he subdues the faculties that grasp at sensory objects and dwells securely in ethical discipline and meditative concentration.
Though having attained the Buddha’s bodhi, He does not abandon the realm of sentient beings;
Practicing that true compassion, He causes them to seek supreme virtue.
These four proclaimed by the Buddhas Will swiftly yield the fruit of the Sugata.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"There are four kinds of transgressions for a bodhisattva. Kāśyapa replied:
"What are the four kinds?
"First, it is a transgression for a bodhisattva to go and convert others when their faculty of faith is not yet mature.
Second, it is a transgression for a bodhisattva to extensively preach the Buddha-dharma to sentient beings who hold inferior and false views."
Third, to preach the Mahāyāna Dharma to sentient beings of the Hīnayāna is a transgression for a bodhisattva;

fourth, to treat with contempt those sentient beings who correctly practice and maintain the precepts, while instead gathering in and accepting those sentient beings who break the precepts and engage in perverse conduct.
Kāśyapa! These four kinds are transgressions of a bodhisattva.
Regarding this, I shall now speak again in verse:
"When sentient beings' faith is not yet matured, one goes there to transform them;
for those inferior and heterodox sentient beings, one extensively expounds the Dharma;
and within the ranks of the śrāvakas, one distinguishes the Mahāyāna teachings."
To treat those who practice correctly with contempt, and to accept those who break the precepts—
knowing these four transgressions, a bodhisattva must distance themselves from them;
if one acts according to these four dharmas, enlightenment will not be attained.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"There are four kinds of dharmas that accomplish the path of a bodhisattva.
Kāśyapa addressed him, saying:
“What are the four dharmas?
First, to maintain equanimity of mind toward all sentient beings;
second, to teach and transform all sentient beings by means of the Buddha’s wisdom.”
Third, to expound the sublime Dharma for all sentient beings;
fourth, to practice correct skillful means toward all sentient beings. Kāśyapa!
These four dharmas accomplish the path of a bodhisattva.
Regarding this, I shall now speak again in verse:
"Towards all classes of sentient beings, One should constantly practice a mind of equanimity;
To instruct all sentient beings, leading them into the wisdom of the Tathāgata;
to constantly expound the subtle and wondrous Dharma, delivering all people;
and to abide securely within reality—this is called right skillful means.
"These four equal dharmas are constantly proclaimed by the Buddha himself;
by practicing them in accordance with the teaching, one accomplishes the path of a bodhisattva.
The Buddha said to Kāśyapa:
“There are four kinds of dharmas that are enemies of a bodhisattva and should not be practiced.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“What are these four dharmas?”
"First, delighting in the practice of the Lesser Vehicle for one's own benefit;
second, practicing the shallow and proximate principles of the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle;
third, conforming to worldly incantations, arts, and crafts."
Fourth, using worldly wisdom and eloquence to collect those worldly, false, and profitless dharmas.
Kāśyapa! These four dharmas are the enemies of a bodhisattva and must not be practiced together with them.
I shall now speak again in verse regarding this:
"If one practices the Śrāvaka vehicle, The conduct of renunciation for one's own benefit;
Or that of the Pratyekabuddhas, The conduct for realizing the shallow principle."
Addicted to worldly arts, such as technical skills and incantations;
further employing worldly wit and sophistry, they vainly collect teachings of no benefit to deceive and mislead sentient beings, never reaching the limit of reality.
"These four types of bodhisattva conduct cause all roots of virtue to be extinguished;
they do not share the same path as one's enemies. The Buddha has said that they should be avoided.
Thus spoke the Buddha to Kāśyapa.
“There are four kinds of dharmas that constitute a bodhisattva’s good friend.
Kāśyapa said: “What are these four dharmas?”
"First, those who seek the path to enlightenment are good friends to a bodhisattva;
second, those who act as great Dharma masters are good friends to a bodhisattva;
third, those who give rise to all roots of goodness through the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation are good friends to a bodhisattva."
Fourth, those who seek all Buddha-dharmas from the Buddha, the World-Honored One, are good friends to a bodhisattva. Kāśyapa,
these four dharmas constitute the good friends of a bodhisattva.
I shall now speak again in verse regarding this:
"For those seeking to achieve enlightenment, The Buddha-sons are their intimate and virtuous friends;
Acting as great Dharma-preachers, They bring forth the wisdom of hearing and reflection."
Transforming and teaching all sentient beings, They give rise to the five roots of goodness;
Constantly being children of the Sugata, They shall attain the path of perfect enlightenment.
The Buddha taught these four dharmas, So that one does not become deluded regarding right practice.
"Causing one to attain great enlightenment—this is called a true and virtuous friend.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"There are four kinds of dharmas that constitute the semblance of a bodhisattva."
Kāśyapa replied, "What are the four dharmas? [The Buddha said:
"First, acting for the sake of gain and honor rather than for the sake of the Dharma;..."
Second, praising others for the sake of gain rather than for their virtuous discipline;
third, seeking one's own benefit and peace while failing to benefit suffering sentient beings;
fourth, failing to give rise to a resolute desire for genuine virtues and capabilities.
Kāśyapa! These four dharmas are the semblances of a bodhisattva.
Regarding this, I shall now speak again in verse:
They widely seek gain and offerings, yet do not listen to or receive the Dharma;
they delight in being praised by others, while abandoning virtuous deeds;
they single-mindedly seek their own peace, showing no compassion for the suffering of sentient beings.
Regarding those [objects of] reality, virtue, and capability, There is neither delight nor conceptualization.
These four kinds of phenomena, The Buddha has declared to be mere images;
You, the assembly of bodhisattvas, Should each and every one distance yourselves from them.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"There are four kinds of dharmas that constitute the true virtues of a bodhisattva.
Kāśyapa addressed him, saying:
“What are the four dharmas?
“First, entering the gate of liberation of emptiness, one has faith that karmic retribution is without intrinsic nature.
Second, entering the gates of selflessness and wishlessness, although one attains nirvāṇa, one constantly gives rise to great compassion and delights in delivering sentient beings.”
Third, skillfully applying expedient means within the great cycle of saṃsāra;
fourth, bestowing gifts upon sentient beings without seeking any karmic reward. Kāśyapa!
These four dharmas constitute the true virtues of a bodhisattva.
Regarding this, I shall now speak again in verse:
"Entering that liberation of emptiness, With faith observing that karma has no intrinsic nature;
Through the gateways of non-self and wishlessness, they abide in the practice of loving-kindness and compassion;
though they have realized the emptiness of nirvāṇa, because they delight in delivering sentient beings,
they skillfully employ various expedient means within that cycle of saṃsāra.
"Extensively saving all living beings, yet not hoping for karmic rewards.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"There are four kinds of dharmas that constitute the great treasury of a bodhisattva."
Kāśyapa replied, "What are the four dharmas? [The Buddha said:
"First, to reverently make offerings to all Buddhas;"
Second, constantly practicing the six great pāramitās;
third, honoring the Dharma masters with a mind that never wavers;
fourth, delighting in dwelling in forest retreats with a mind free from distraction.
Kāśyapa! These four dharmas constitute the great treasury of a bodhisattva.
Regarding this, I shall now speak again in verse:
"In the presence of those Buddhas, I made offerings to all the Buddhas;
among the six perfections of the Mahāyāna, I practiced the pāramitās;
I honored the teachers of the Dharma and served them with a mind that never retreated."
"Always dwelling in forests and wilds, pure and free from confusion—
these four are taught by the Sugatas as the great Dharma-treasury of the Buddha’s sons.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
“There are four kinds of dharmas that keep one far removed from the bodhisattva’s path of Māra.
Kāśyapa said: “What are these four dharmas?”
"First, all practices one undertakes are not divorced from the bodhicitta;
second, one’s mind harbors no malice or harm toward any sentient being;
third, one clearly understands and penetrates all dharmas."
Fourth, one does not give rise to contempt for any sentient being. Kāśyapa,
these four dharmas keep a bodhisattva far removed from the path of Māra.
I shall now repeat these verses here:
"Whatever various virtuous deeds one performs, One does not depart from the bodhicitta;
Toward all those living beings, One is at all times free from affliction and harm."
Thoroughly penetrating all phenomena;
abandoning all contempt for living beings—
these four, taught by the Sugata, lead one far away from the paths of Māra.
By practicing according to this, such a person attains the limit of that true emptiness.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
“There are four kinds of dharmas that gather all the roots of goodness of a bodhisattva.”
Kāśyapa replied, "What are these four dharmas? [The Buddha said:
"First, delighting in dwelling in the forest in quietude and silence;"
Second, gathering all sentient beings through the four means of attraction—generosity, kind speech, beneficial conduct, and cooperation;
third, joyfully seeking the sublime Dharma even at the cost of one's body and life;
fourth, never being satiated with hearing the meaning [of the Dharma] and diligently practicing vigor to accumulate all roots of goodness.
Kāśyapa! These four dharmas can gather all the roots of goodness of a bodhisattva.
Now, regarding this, I shall speak again in verse:
"Delighting in dwelling in secluded places, remaining in silent composure free from clamor and vexation;
governing sentient beings through the four means of integration, causing them to ascend the path to enlightenment;
diligently seeking the wondrous Dharma, casting aside even body and life;"
"Exerting diligence to accumulate roots of goodness, Listening to the Dharma with a mind never satiated—
The Buddha has taught these four practices, Which give birth to boundless goodness.
The Buddha addressed Kāśyapa:
“There are four kinds of dharmas that give rise to the immeasurable merit of a bodhisattva.
Kāśyapa said: “What are these four dharmas?”
"First, constantly practicing the gift of Dharma with a mind free from stinginess;
second, giving rise to great compassion to rescue and protect sentient beings who have broken the precepts;
third, transforming all sentient beings so that they resolve to attain Bodhicitta."
Fourth, to exercise patience toward and protect those who are base and wicked. Kāśyapa!
These four dharmas give rise to the immeasurable merit of a bodhisattva.
I shall now speak again in verse regarding this:
"Extensively expounding all sublime dharmas with a pure mind free from stinginess;
Bestowing compassion and protection upon all sentient beings who violate the precepts."
Causing those classes of sentient beings to give rise to the mind of pure awakening;
protecting various inferior and wicked people through the practice of patience—
Bodhisattvas and all Buddhas practice these four deeds together.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"There are four kinds of dharmas that can destroy the ignorance and afflictions within the mental ground of a bodhisattva. Kāśyapa said:
“What are the four dharmas?
“First, the fulfillment of the precepts practiced without transgression;
second, upholding the sublime Dharma with body and mind free from weariness.”
Third, to transmit and bestow the lamp of the Dharma according to their respective understandings;
fourth, to pay homage with sincere devotion and extol the virtues of the Buddha. Kāśyapa!
These four dharmas can destroy the ignorance and afflictions of the bodhisattva’s mental ground.
Regarding this, I shall now speak again in verse:
“Firmly maintaining the complete precepts, The mental ground remains free from transgression.”
Constantly upholding the wondrous Dharma, with a mind untiring day and night;
explaining all the teachings of the Buddhas according to their inclinations, bestowing the lamp of the Dharma;
praising all Buddhas and prostrating with sincere devotion.
"The wise who practice these four Can sever the ground of ignorance;
All sons of the Buddhas Rely on these to attain bodhi.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
“There are four kinds of dharmas that give rise to the unimpeded wisdom of a bodhisattva.
Kāśyapa said: “What are these four dharmas?”
"First, the giving of the Dharma;
second, upholding the sublime Dharma;
third, not harming others."
Fourth, one should not be arrogant or contemptuous. Kāśyapa,
these four dharmas give rise to the unimpeded wisdom of a bodhisattva.
I shall now repeat this in verse:
"The sublime gift of Dharma that one practices, Causes others to receive and uphold it;
One does not envy the learning of sentient beings, But respects those who maintain the precepts."
The four dharmas eliminate past offenses and bring about the attainment of supreme enlightenment;
by relying on these one attains bodhi and gives rise to unimpeded wisdom.
Furthermore, through the twelve distinct practices, the wise attain bodhi.
Having attained the flavor of the nectar of immortality and possessing the profound eye of Dharma, those who explain, recite, and uphold it—
of such persons the Buddha says that the merit they obtain is immeasurable.
If one were to fill as many Buddha-fields as there are grains of sand in the Ganges with the seven precious jewels and offer them to all Buddhas,
that merit would likewise be immeasurable;
If a person recollects this Dharma, even a single four-line verse, their merit shall surpass that [of the former].
Furthermore, Kāśyapa, if one upholds these four lines,
even if they are not yet called a bodhisattva, they shall be named a bodhisattva.

The Dharma-transmitting Master, Your Servant Shi Hu, translates by imperial decree: The Buddha addressed Kāśyapa:
"If Bodhisattvas are fully endowed with thirty-two qualities, they are called 'Bodhisattvas'."
Kāśyapa said, “What are these thirty-two qualities? [The Buddha replied:
“They are that which brings benefit to all sentient beings and serves as the seed for the knowledge of all-knowledge.”
Without discriminating between the noble and the humble, they cause them to attain wisdom;
for the sake of all sentient beings, they humble their minds and remain free from self-attachment;
with true compassion, their resolve never regresses.
Maintaining equanimity of mind toward both virtuous friends and evil friends;
even upon reaching nirvana, one continues to contemplate kind speech;
greeting others with a welcoming disposition and taking compassion for those burdened by heavy loads.
They constantly give rise to compassion for all sentient beings;
they always seek the sublime Dharma with a mind free from weariness;
and they never feel satiety in hearing the Dharma.
Constantly examine one's own faults and do not speak of the transgressions of others;
maintain all dignified deportment and always give rise to the great resolve;
cultivate all supreme deeds without seeking their karmic rewards.
The virtue of the precepts thus produced extinguishes all saṃsāra;
it causes the aspiration for the Path to increase in all sentient beings;
and it brings about the complete accumulation and practice of all roots of goodness.
Although they practice patience and diligence as if entering formless meditative absorptions;
they possess wisdom and skillful means, being well-versed in dhāraṇīs;
and they constantly practice the four means of attraction with clever expedients.
Maintaining precepts and violating precepts are non-dual through a mind of loving-kindness;
constantly dwelling in mountain forests, one delights in inquiring about the profound Dharma;
and one feels weary detachment toward all the various things in the world.
One delights in the supramundane, unconditioned fruits and virtues;
one distances oneself from the practices of the Lesser Vehicle and pursues the Great Vehicle;
and one abandons evil friends while drawing near to virtuous friends.
Having attained complete mastery over the four immeasurables and the five supernormal powers, they have purified all ignorance;
they do not cling to what is false or true but rely upon a teacher according to reality;
and they have generated the bodhicitta that is pure and unadulterated.
Kāśyapa! One who is thus endowed with these thirty-two dharmas is called a bodhisattva.
Now, regarding this, I shall speak again in verse:
"To benefit all sentient beings, Desiring to practice pure conduct,
To cause them to give birth to all-encompassing wisdom, Without discriminating between noble and base,
May they equally enter the wisdom of the Tathāgata; Truly pitying sentient beings,"
With a mind that does not regress, one views both good friends and evil friends with equanimity; even when reaching nirvana,
one first greets others with kind words and feels compassion for those burdened by heavy loads.
And toward all those sentient beings, may he never cease his great compassion;
seeking the Dharma with a heart free from weariness, hearing the meaning of the teachings he is never satiated;
constantly reflecting upon his own faults, he does not revile the transgressions of others.
Fully cultivating all modes of dignified conduct, One gives rise to the practice of the Mahāyāna;
Seeking no karmic retribution, The virtues of the precepts one maintains Bring about the cessation of saṃsāra, Causing all those sentient beings...
Keeping far from harm, they increase the resolve for the Way; through patience, they accumulate roots of goodness;
with diligence, they cultivate all practices as if entering the formless concentrations;
through wisdom and various skillful means, they master and well-understand the dhāraṇīs.
Constantly practicing the four means of attraction, Compassionate toward both those who uphold and those who violate the precepts,
Always dwelling amidst the forest groves, Ever delighting in hearing the profound Dharma,
Feeling weary of and detached from the world, And cherishing and revering the unsurpassed fruit.
Distant from the Śrāvaka vehicle, they cultivate the practices of the Mahāyāna;
abandoning evil companions, they draw near to virtuous friends;
possessing the five supernormal powers and the four immeasurables, their wisdom fully penetrates all things.
Pure and utterly free from ignorance, Unattached to either the false or the true,
One relies on a teacher to investigate reality, Practicing with single-minded purity and without distraction.

the Bodhisattva will fulfill their practice and obtain the nectar-like flavor of Buddhahood.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"I shall speak a parable for the sake of the bodhisattvas, so that they may come to know and see the virtues of a bodhisattva.
Kāśyapa said, "What is the meaning of this?"

“Kāśyapa! It is like the element of earth, which serves as the support for all sentient beings and causes them to grow and flourish, yet that element of earth has no seeking or craving toward those beings.”

So too it is with the Bodhisattva: from the first generation of the mind until sitting at the site of enlightenment to attain Bodhi, throughout that interval, they ferry across all sentient beings without attachment or seeking, and it is likewise thus.
I shall now speak a verse on this matter:
"Just as the element of earth Serves as the support and nourishment for all sentient beings,
Yet toward those beings it has no seeking and no attachment."
From the first generation of the mind of enlightenment until reaching the site of awakening,
one attains unsurpassed enlightenment and delivers sentient beings; without seeking or craving, without enmity or attachment,
one impartially gathers them in, causing them to attain Bodhi.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"For example, just as the element of water moistens and benefits all medicinal herbs, trees, and forests, yet that element of water has neither affection nor seeking toward those plants and trees."

Kāśyapa! It is the same for a bodhisattva: with a pure mind of loving-kindness, they act universally toward all sentient beings, moistening and benefiting the seeds of the white dharmas within them, causing them to grow without attachment or seeking.
I shall now speak a verse on this matter:
"Just as the element of water Moistens and benefits all things, Causing medicinal herbs, trees,
and forests to grow, Yet it has no attachment and makes no request."
With a pure and compassionate mind, pervading all sentient beings, one universally moistens them in succession;
as the seeds of purity increase, one destroys the powerful Māra and attains the Bodhi of the Buddha.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"It is like the element of fire, which ripens all grains, wheat, and crops; yet the element of fire has no attachment to them and makes no request for them."
Kāśyapa! It is the same with the bodhisattva, who brings all the sprouts of virtue in sentient beings to maturity through great wisdom.
Regarding this, I shall now speak in verse:
"Just as the fire element ripens all five kinds of grain and crops,
yet that fire element has no seeking and no attachment toward those crops."
The Bodhisattva is likewise; with the fire of wisdom, he brings to maturity all the sprouts of virtue in sentient beings, yet toward them, the Bodhisattva has no seeking and no attachment.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa: "Kāśyapa,
it is like the element of wind, which pervades all buddha-fields."
The Bodhisattva is likewise; through skillful means, they cause all within the realm of sentient beings to understand the Buddha-dharma.
Regarding this, I shall now speak in verse:
"Just as the element of wind, By its own power, Pervades the entire Buddha-field."
The assembly of bodhisattvas is likewise; through skillful means, they preach the supreme Dharma for those sons of the Buddha.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
“For example, when Māra the Foe leads his fourfold army, the gods of the desire realm cannot subdue him. Kāśyapa!”
The Bodhisattva is likewise; having attained purity of mind, no Māras whatsoever can delude or disturb them.
Now, regarding this, I shall speak in verse:
"Just as the Enemy Māra, Leading his fourfold army, And the various devas of the Desire Realm..."
They cannot subdue them;
so it is with the Bodhisattva: having attained purity of mind, all Māras cannot delude or disturb him.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
“It is like the waxing moon, which gradually increases until it becomes full. Kāśyapa!”
The Bodhisattva is likewise; with an undefiled mind, they seek all dharmas until they reach fulfillment.
Regarding this, I shall now speak in verse:
"Just as the bright moon, Gradually increases Until it reaches fullness."
The Bodhisattva is likewise: with an undefiled mind, seeking to cultivate all virtues, they gradually advance until the white dharmas are perfected.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"It is like the rising sun that emits a great radiance, illuminating this world so that there is nothing that is not made bright. Kāśyapa!"
The Bodhisattva is likewise; emitting the light of wisdom, they illuminate all sentient beings, such that none remain unenlightened.
Regarding this, I shall now speak in verse:
"Just as when the sun rises, It illuminates that world, And all forms and images..."
There is nothing that is not made clear.
So too it is with the Bodhisattva: emitting the light of wisdom, they illuminate all sentient beings, such that there are none who do not attain understanding and liberation.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"For example, the lion, the king of beasts, possesses great majestic power; wherever he goes, he is neither startled nor terrified."
Kāśyapa! It is the same for the bodhisattva: dwelling securely in the virtue of extensive learning and ethical discipline, they are neither startled nor terrified by anything wherever they go.
Regarding this, I shall now speak a verse:
"The lion, king of beasts, possesses majestic power and valor; wherever he goes, his mind knows no fear.
Likewise, one who upholds the precepts and wisdom, wherever they go within that world,"
"Free from all fears.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"It is like a dragon-elephant of great power, which carries all manner of heavy burdens without experiencing fatigue or distress."
Kāśyapa, it is the same for the bodhisattva: though they shoulder the sufferings of the five aggregates of all sentient beings, they do not experience those sufferings as their own.
Now, regarding this, I shall speak in verse:
"Just as a dragon-elephant possesses great power and can carry heavy burdens upon its back without experiencing fatigue or suffering,
so too is the Bodhisattva: though he carries the five aggregates and all the sufferings of sentient beings, he likewise experiences no fatigue or suffering."
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"It is like a lotus flower; though it grows in water amidst mud and turbid water, it cannot be defiled by them. Kāśyapa!"
The Bodhisattva is likewise; though born into the world, the defilements of the world can never adhere to him.
Regarding this, I shall now speak in verse:
"Just as a lotus flower, born from within the water, is not stained by the turbid water or the mud."
Yet it cannot be defiled.
So too is the Bodhisattva: although born into the world amidst its various defilements, he cannot be attached to them.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
“It is as if, for example, someone were to skillfully cut down a tree but not its roots, so that later on it grows again from the great earth. Kāśyapa!”

The Bodhisattva is likewise: by the power of skillful means, he cuts off those afflictions without severing their seeds, and through the roots of goodness of great compassion, he is reborn within the triple world.
Regarding this, I shall now speak in verse:
"Just as a person, by means of skillful means, cuts down the trunk of a tree..."
If one does not cut the roots of a tree, it will grow again upon the great earth at a later time.
So too it is with the Bodhisattva: by means of skillful means, they sever those afflictions but do not destroy their seeds;
because of great compassion, they are born again within the triple world.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa: "Kāśyapa,
it is like the rivers flowing from all directions that all return to the great ocean, becoming of one and the same salty taste."
The Bodhisattva is likewise: all roots of goodness and various benefits dedicated toward Bodhi converge with Nirvana in a single, identical flavor.
I shall now speak a verse concerning this:
"Just as all the waters of the rivers and streams enter the great ocean and become of one salty taste."
"The benefits of roots of goodness are dedicated toward bodhi and that true limit (bhūtakoṭi),
all returning to a single flavor.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Just as the Four Great Heavenly Kings and the hosts of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven must dwell upon Mount Sumeru,
Kāśyapa, so it is with the Bodhisattva: the wholesome dharmas cultivated for the sake of omniscience must dwell within the great mind of enlightenment."
I shall now speak of this in verse:
"Just as the Four Great Kings, And the hosts of Śakra, Must abide upon Mount Sumeru."
"So too is the bodhisattva: for the sake of all-knowledge, they dwell securely in enlightenment through the wholesome dharmas they have cultivated.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"It is like a king who, wishing to carry out the affairs of state, must rely upon his ministers."
Kāśyapa! It is the same for a bodhisattva: wishing to perform the work of a Buddha, one must rely upon wisdom and skillful means.
I shall now speak a verse concerning this:
"Just as a king who wishes to carry out the affairs of state must rely upon his ministers to achieve success,
so too it is with a bodhisattva: wishing to perform the deeds of a Buddha, they depend upon skillful means and wisdom to achieve certain accomplishment."
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
“Kāśyapa, it is like a clear sky free from clouds and mist; in such a world, there will ultimately be no sign of rain falling.”
The Bodhisattva is likewise; one who has heard little and possesses little wisdom will never have the appearance of preaching the Dharma to sentient beings.
Regarding this, I shall now speak in verse:
"Just as the sky, Clear and free from clouds and mist, Within that world..."
In the end, no rain falls.
So it is with the bodhisattva who has heard little and possesses little wisdom; toward sentient beings, he lacks the appearance of one who teaches the Dharma.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
“It is like when great clouds and thunder arise in space; they will surely bring down sweet rain to ripen the crops. Kāśyapa!”
The Bodhisattva is likewise: he raises clouds of compassion within this world and lets fall the rain of the sublime Dharma to bring sentient beings to maturity.
Regarding this, I shall now speak in verse:
"Just as when clouds and thunder suddenly arise in the void, There will surely be a descent of sweet rain."
Just as it brings crops to maturity, so too does the Bodhisattva: spreading the clouds of universal compassion and pouring down the rain of Dharma, they bring sentient beings to maturity.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa: “Kāśyapa,
it is like a wheel-turning sage king, who has seven treasures that constantly follow him wherever he goes.”
The Bodhisattva is likewise; the seven factors of enlightenment constantly follow him.
Regarding this, I shall now speak in verse:
"Just as in the world, the Wheel-Turning Sage King possesses the seven treasures,"
They constantly follow the king’s movements.
So too it is with the Bodhisattva: wherever he goes, the seven factors of enlightenment follow after him.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"For example, it is like a maṇi jewel that brings great wealth and honor, its value being as much as hundreds of thousands of kārṣāpaṇas in wealth and honor."
Kāśyapa! It is the same for a bodhisattva: they obtain the price of great wealth, which is worth hundreds of thousands times the wealth of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Regarding this, I shall now speak a verse:
"Just as a mani jewel, when obtained in great abundance,
cannot be compared to hundreds of thousands of kārṣāpaṇas;
so too is the Bodhisattva— his wealth and nobility are manifold and vast."
"Even the pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas, numbering in the hundreds of thousands, cannot be compared to them.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"For example, it is like the hosts of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven who dwell in the Miśrakāvana Grove; they enjoy wealth and nobility with equal parity, without distinction."
Kāśyapa! It is the same for a bodhisattva: if they abide in a pure mind, they employ upright skillful means for the sake of all sentient beings, which are impartial and non-dual.
Regarding this, I shall now speak in verse:
"Just as those who dwell in the Caitraratha Grove in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven enjoy wealth and honor with equal impartiality and without distinction,
so too it is for the Bodhisattva who dwells in a pure mind."
"Uprightness for the sake of all living beings, and skillful means are likewise non-dual.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"It is like a person who is expertly skilled in incantations and well-versed in poisons; no poison whatsoever can cause them harm."
Kāśyapa! It is the same for a bodhisattva: being endowed with great wisdom and skillfully practicing expedient means, no afflictions can cause them harm.
Now, regarding this, I shall speak in verse:
"Just as people in the world who are well-versed in medicinal herbs and incantations cannot be harmed by any poisons or the like,
so too is the Bodhisattva: if they possess skillful means and wisdom,"
"All the poisons of affliction cannot cause them harm.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"For example, in this world, a soil of manure can produce lush and flourishing sugarcane."
Kāśyapa! It is the same with the bodhisattva: even when situated in the dung-heap of afflictions, they are able to produce the seeds of all-knowledge.
Now, regarding this, I shall speak a verse:
"Just as sugarcane grows from a field of manure, Thriving and flourishing far beyond the ordinary;
So too is the meaning of this: When a bodhisattva dwells amidst afflictions, They give birth to all-encompassing wisdom."
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
“Kāśyapa, it is like a person who has not trained in martial arts; if he were to take up a weapon, would he know how to employ it? Kāśyapa!

The Bodhisattva is likewise: having previously not heard the Dharma and possessing little knowledge of the faculties and medicines [of sentient beings], if he clings to his own wisdom and views, how could he distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"It is like a potter who, wishing to fire ceramic vessels, must use a great fire."
Kāśyapa! It is the same for a bodhisattva: wishing to awaken the wisdom of ignorant and deluded sentient beings, one must employ the fire of the Buddha-dharma’s wisdom. Kāśyapa!

All such phenomena as the wholesome and the unwholesome, the mundane and the supramundane, the faulty and the faultless, the outflowing and the non-outflowing, the conditioned and the unconditioned, and those with afflictions and those without afflictions.

I say to you: with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form arise; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases arise; with the six sense bases as condition, contact arises; with contact as condition, feeling arises; with feeling as condition, craving arises; with craving as condition, clinging arises; with clinging as condition, existence arises; with existence as condition, birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair arise.
Kāśyapa! Thus is this great mass of suffering accumulated. With the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease;

with the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases; with the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form ceases; with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease; with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases; with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases; with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases; with the cessation of craving, clinging ceases; with the cessation of clinging, existence ceases; with the cessation of existence, birth ceases; with the cessation of birth, aging and death cease; and with the cessation of aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair cease.
In this way, there is the cessation of this entire great mass of suffering.
Kāśyapa, when one observes with wisdom that illumination and ignorance are equal and lack these two characteristics, [this occurs].
Kāśyapa! One should observe the dharmas within these reflections as they truly are.

In this way, with the cessation of formations, there is the cessation of formations; in this way, with the cessation of consciousness, there is the cessation of consciousness; in this way, with the cessation of name-and-form, there is the cessation of name-and-form; in this way, with the cessation of the six sense bases, there is the cessation of the six sense bases; in this way, with the cessation of contact, there is the cessation of contact; in this way, with the cessation of feeling, there is the cessation of feeling; in this way, with the cessation of craving, there is the cessation of craving; in this way, with the cessation of clinging, there is the cessation of clinging; in this way, with the cessation of existence, there is the cessation of existence; in this way, with the cessation of birth, there is the cessation of birth; in this way, with the cessation of aging-and-death, there is the cessation of aging-and-death.
Thus, through the wisdom that contemplates the nature of arising and the nature of cessation as being non-dual in character. Kāśyapa!
Free from these two characteristics, this is called the contemplation of phenomena within the reflected image according to reality.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa, one should correctly contemplate the phenomena within the reflected image; those phenomena are neither empty nor non-empty.

Such empty phenomena have no characteristic of existence, nor do they have a characteristic of non-existence. The characteristic of phenomena is itself the characteristic of emptiness; the characteristic of emptiness is itself the signless; the signless is itself the wishless."
Why is this? Because there is nothing to be willed or produced; the signless is itself the mark of emptiness.
For a practitioner who acts in this way, if a dharma has not yet arisen, it does not arise, because that dharma has not yet arisen.
Just as that phenomenon arises, it does not arise [as a substantial entity], because once arisen, it has already passed away.
Thus, through the non-arising of arising and the relinquishing of grasping, phenomena lack intrinsic nature; that which lacks intrinsic nature is emptiness.
Thus one correctly contemplates these dharmas spoken of as images.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa, the person (pudgala) is not an emptiness resulting from destruction; its very essence is emptiness, for it was originally non-existent."
"It is not that the past is empty, nor that the future is empty; the present itself is empty.
Kāśyapa replied, "Regarding that *pudgala*, I now realize and know it to be empty, for it has destroyed my [self-attachment]."
"All things are empty; such is the nature of these dharmas. The Buddha said, "Kāśyapa!"
What you say is incorrect. Kāśyapa!

"Will this person be able to escape the illness? Kāśyapa replied, "No."
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha said, “What do you think?”
“World-Honored One!
Because this person’s illness is grave, it cannot be cured.
The Buddha said:

"Just as when a person with a grave illness is made to take excellent medicine, yet the illness does not recede despite taking it—that person cannot be cured.
Clinging to emptiness is likewise; in all such cases,"
"One who is deeply attached to the view of emptiness—I say that such a person is incurable.

"Why is this? For fear that the void might fall to the ground and injure your body.

If those deluded śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas are likewise so, they will feel fear and terror upon hearing the Dharma of emptiness.

yet these people, being themselves deluded and ignorant, give rise to groundless fear.

The Buddha told Kāśyapa:

I shall now speak a verse regarding this:
"Just as a skilled painter, While painting a fierce yakṣa,

I shall now speak a verse regarding this:
"Just as a conjurer can transform illusory beings,
and those illusory beings can likewise transform the conjurer."
"The bhikṣu who practices in accordance [with the Dharma] generates the resolve in this same way:
he speaks of all things as empty, and he also speaks of emptiness itself as being without reality.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
“Just as when two pieces of wood are rubbed together and wind blows forth fire, once the fire has arisen it burns those two pieces of wood;
Kāśyapa, so too is the case with right contemplation: from the path of right view the faculty of wisdom arises, and once the faculty of wisdom has arisen, it burns that right contemplation.”
I shall now speak a verse on this matter:
"Just as when two pieces of wood are rubbed together, The wind blows and that fire is produced;
In the very instant the fire arises, It in turn consumes both pieces of wood."
Right contemplation is also like this: it can give rise to the faculty of wisdom;
yet in the very moment that [wisdom] arises, it in turn burns up right contemplation.

The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"For example, the light of a lamp can destroy all darkness; yet from where does that darkness depart?"
It does not go to the east, it does not go to the south, it does not go to the west, and it does not go to the north.
Its going is not going, and its coming is not coming.
“Kāśyapa! Furthermore, the light of a lamp is not something that can destroy darkness by its own power.
Moreover, if there were no darkness, what would the light of a lamp manifest?”
Kāśyapa! The light of a lamp and darkness originally have no self-nature; both of these are empty, with nothing to be attained and nothing to be abandoned. Kāśyapa!
In this same way, wisdom is also like this: when wisdom arises, ignorance is immediately abandoned; yet where does that ignorance go?
It does not go to the east, it does not go to the south, it does not go to the west, and it does not go to the north.
Going is not going, and coming is not coming.
"Kāśyapa, furthermore, when wisdom arises, ignorance is immediately abandoned; it is not that my wisdom can destroy his ignorance."
Furthermore, if ignorance were fundamentally non-existent, how could wisdom manifest? Kāśyapa!
Both wisdom and ignorance lack intrinsic nature; both are empty, with nothing to be attained and nothing to be relinquished.
I shall now speak a verse on this matter:
"Just as a lamp's light is able to dispel the darkness,
when that darkness is extinguished and vanishes, it goes nowhere in any direction."
Furthermore, if this lamp-light were not for darkness it could not be manifested;
both lack intrinsic nature, and being without nature, both are empty.
Wisdom is also like this: when wisdom arises,
"To abandon through ignorance—these two are like flowers in the sky;
both lack intrinsic nature, and thus neither grasping nor abandoning can be found.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"It is like an empty house with no doors or windows, where for a hundred or a thousand years no person has lived.
The chamber is pitch-black, yet suddenly a celestial being lights a lamp within that house."
Kāśyapa, what do you think?
This darkness has remained here for hundreds or thousands of years; I shall not depart from it now.
"Is such a thing possible? Kāśyapa replied, "No."
“World-Honored One!
That darkness is powerless; if a lamp-light is produced, it must certainly depart.
The Buddha said:
“Kāśyapa! Those karmas and afflictions are likewise; they remain within that consciousness for hundreds of thousands of kalpas.
Yet, if a practitioner, for even a single day and night, dwells in correct contemplation and gives rise to the lamp of wisdom, [they are extinguished].”
Kāśyapa! When such a faculty of wisdom arises in a noble one, these karmas and afflictions will certainly not exist.
Regarding this, I shall now speak in verse:
"Just as a house that has stood for a hundred thousand years, devoid of people and lacking doors or windows,
might suddenly have a god or a human kindle a lamp within it—
so too does this long-enduring darkness vanish in a single instant."
Just as one leaves a house in darkness, saying, "I shall not dwell here for long;
I will depart from this place," so too is the meaning of this:
though one may dwell for hundreds of thousands of eons, [the mind does not abide].
Their intrinsic nature is not real;
entering correctly into the contemplation of suchness, the lamp of wisdom arises in brilliant splendor,
and those accumulations of afflictions cannot remain for even a single moment.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
“For example, Kāśyapa, just as space does not abide in seeds.”
Thus, if that practitioner is firmly attached to the view of annihilationism—holding that the past has already ceased and the future does not exist—how can the seed of the Buddha-dharma abide?
Regarding this, I shall now speak in verse:
"Just as the great empty space, Is boundless and immeasurable,"
If a person were in mid-air, where could they plant seeds?
The view of nihilism is likewise: the past cannot exist, the future will not arise, and in the present there is no seed of the Buddha-dharma.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
“Suppose the entire earth were filled with dung; it would be possible to plant all kinds of seeds therein.
Kāśyapa, in the same way, when the world is filled with the dung of karma and afflictions, it is possible to plant all the seeds of the Buddha-dharma.”
I shall now speak a verse concerning this:
"Just as the earth and its manure Are suitable for planting wherever they may be;

"If a son of the Buddha draws near, he may plant the seeds of the Buddha-dharma.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"For example, just as lotuses cannot be planted upon salty, barren land."
Kāśyapa! Thus, that which is of the nature of non-action has fundamentally never existed and will not arise in the future; how, then, could it possess the seed of bodhi?
Regarding this, I shall now speak in verse:
"Just as a lotus cannot grow on salty land, yet in the mud and water it arises with most fragrant scent; so too is the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*):

Kāśyapa! Even those sentient beings who engage in afflictions and wrong conduct can give rise to the seed of the Buddha’s Dharma and its wisdom.
Regarding this, I shall now speak in verse:
"Just as a lotus flower can grow from ground of mud and filth,
so too can the seeds of the Buddha-dharma arise within sentient beings who engage in unwholesome actions.

“Kāśyapa, it is like the waters of the four great oceans, vast and boundless.
In the same way, Kāśyapa,

I shall now speak a verse concerning this:
"Just as the four great oceans, Are vast, boundless, and overflowing, So too is the Bodhisattva;

The Buddha told Kāśyapa:

"Just as if one were to take a single hair-tip from a person’s head and divide it into a hundred parts,

"By means of the roots of goodness one has cultivated oneself, one seeks to achieve unsurpassed enlightenment.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"It is like an insect inside a mustard seed that, while eating that mustard seed, perceives the interior of the seed as being like empty space."
Kāśyapa! In this same way, the limited wisdom cultivated by śrāvakas perceives that emptiness of arising;
it is just like this. Now, regarding this, I shall speak a verse:
"Just as within a mustard seed there is a mustard-seed-eating insect that perceives what is unobstructed within it as empty space,
so too the wisdom cultivated by the śrāvakas realizes but a single portion of emptiness."
"What is seen is not large; its meaning is likewise so.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"It is like a person who sees that the space throughout the worlds of the ten directions is boundless."
Kāśyapa! In this way, the dharma-realm perceived by the unimpeded great wisdom of a bodhisattva is likewise without limit.
I shall now speak a verse concerning this:
"Just as the realm of space, throughout the ten directions,
has no boundaries, and all worlds depend upon it without obstruction;
so too is the Bodhisattva, whose supreme wisdom arises."
"Illuminatively perceive the emptiness of the dharma-realm, Boundless and unattainable.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Suppose there is a Kṣatriya consecrated as a king, and that king’s queen secretly consorts with a commoner and subsequently gives birth to a son."
Kāśyapa! What do you think?
Would the son thus born be called a prince of consecration?
Kāśyapa replied, “No, World-Honored One.”
He said, “Kāśyapa!
Those śrāvakas who have attained the realm of non-arising dharma are likewise my consecrated sons, the Tathāgata.”
I shall now speak a verse on this matter:
"The Queen of the King of the Realm, If she has a private union with a commoner,
And subsequently gives birth to a son, He is not called a consecrated prince."
The śrāvakas are likewise: having abandoned desire and realized non-arising, they practice solely for their own benefit;
they are not like the Tathāgata’s consecrated Dharma-princes, the sons of the Buddha who practice both self-benefit and the benefit of others.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Suppose there is a kṣatriya consecrated as king who has a close attendant maidservant whom he favors; she later gives birth to a son."
"Kāśyapa, what do you think?
Would the son born of this maidservant be called a prince? Kāśyapa replied:
“This is a prince. “Kāśyapa!

In the same way, although a bodhisattva who has first resolved for awakening possesses only weak power on the path and cannot yet transform those sentient beings, nor is he yet free from saṃsāra, he may still be called a son of the Tathāgata.”
I shall now speak a verse on this matter:
"Just as the maidservant of a Wheel-Turning King, Having been favored by the King,
later gives birth to a son, Who is likewise a son of the Kṣatriya caste."
The Bodhisattva is also like this: having first resolved upon bodhicitta, their virtuous conduct may be weak and inferior;
yet through skillful means they transform sentient beings, and though they have not yet emerged from the triple world, their deeds accord with the Buddha’s heart.
"they shall be called true sons of the Buddha.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"For example, when a Wheel-Turning King (cakravartin) fathers a thousand sons who are powerful, courageous, eloquent, and handsome, they must possess the marks of a Wheel-Turning King."
“Kāśyapa, if among those sons within his harem there is not even one who possesses the marks of a wheel-turning monarch, that wheel-turning monarch does not regard them as his own children.”

In this way, even if the Tathāgata’s assembly were surrounded by hundreds of thousands of koṭis of śrāvakas, yet lacked even a single person with the marks of a bodhisattva, the Tathāgata would not regard them as his children.
I shall now speak a verse on this matter:
"Just as when a Wheel-Turning King has begotten a thousand princes,
if not even a single son among them possesses the marks of such a Wheel-Turning King,"
This is not the portion of a king; the king has no thought of them as his own sons.
It is the same for the Son of the Buddha: though surrounded by a retinue of a thousand koṭis of śrāvakas, there is not a single one who bears the marks of a bodhisattva.
The Sugata observes that person and does not regard them as a son of the Buddha.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
“For example, when the queen of a universal monarch (cakravartin) becomes pregnant, she will certainly give birth to a prince endowed with the marks of a universal monarch after seven nights.”

While he was in the womb, at the stage of the *kalala* when the major organs and physical forms had not yet developed, gods and humans conceived a heart of deep affection and reverence for him, even though his form was not yet complete;
it was not because they loved that child’s valor or great strength.
"What do you think?
Do they hold that royal lineage of the wheel-turning monarchs in high regard so that it shall not be severed? Kāśyapa!"

It is likewise so: although a bodhisattva who has first resolved for awakening has roots that are not yet matured and has not yet escaped saṃsāra, because they delight in practicing the Buddha-dharma, the Buddhas of the past regard them with love and esteem;

Why is this? It is because they ensure that the Buddha-seed of those bodhisattvas who have first resolved upon enlightenment shall not be severed.
Regarding this, I now speak these verses:
"Just as when the queen of a wheel-turning monarch is pregnant,
though the form has not yet developed after seven days, gods and humans feel love and protection for her;
it is not because of her own great valor or power, but because she bears the lineage of the wheel-turning monarch."
The Bodhisattva is likewise: when first generating the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*) with the desire to deliver beings from saṃsāra,
all the Tathāgatas of the past pay him reverence, for this person shall carry on the work of the Buddhas.
"Among the assembly of śrāvakas, those who correctly contemplate the eight liberations do not give rise to reverence or affection; they lack the portion for attaining buddhahood.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
“Suppose, for example, there were a heap of counterfeit mani-gems and lapis lazuli as large as Mount Sumeru; it would not equal a single genuine mani-gem or lapis lazuli treasure.
Kāśyapa, in the same way, even if all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas were gathered together, they could not equal a single bodhisattva who has first resolved to attain awakening.”
I shall now speak a verse on this matter:
"Just as if there were a heap of imitation lapis lazuli And those mani-jewels piled up like Mount Sumeru, They would not equal a single genuine mani."

Even if there were as many śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas as there are motes of dust, they would not equal those who have first resolved their minds upon enlightenment, even a single jewel of lapis lazuli.
"One who seeks that Bodhi is a single individual among Bodhisattvas.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"For example, when the kalaviṅka bird dwells within its egg, it is already distinct from all other winged creatures."
Kāśyapa, what do you think?
It is because one shall produce all manner of exquisite and beautiful sounds.
Kāśyapa, in this way,

although that bodhisattva who has first resolved upon enlightenment dwells within the storehouse of karma, afflictions, and ignorance, he is already not to be equated with any śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha.
Kāśyapa, what do you think?
It is because they possess the skillful means of teaching the Dharma through roots of goodness dedicated toward awakening.
I shall now speak a verse regarding this:
"Just as a *kalaviṅka* bird, while dwelling within its egg, though its physical form is not yet visible, is distinct from all other birds; "
When one utters a beautiful sound, it causes people to always feel love and joy.

He dedicates [merit] toward great peace and happiness, employing skillful means to benefit sentient beings;
with a stainless mind of compassion, he is able to proclaim sublime sounds.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
“It is like a prince born of the queen of a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin), who possesses the auspicious marks of a wheel-turning monarch; all kings and the common people alike submit to him.”
Kāśyapa! Thus, all sentient beings in the heavens and among humans submit to and follow such a bodhisattva who has first resolved their mind toward enlightenment.
Regarding this, I shall now speak in verse:
"Just as the son born of the queen of a wheel-turning monarch,
though still a child, possesses the full marks of royal fortune;
thus all kings, ministers, and subjects alike turn toward him in devotion."
The Bodhisattva is also like this: from the first moment they resolve upon bodhicitta, they are endowed with the marks of a Son of the Buddha;

"It is like the great king of snow mountains, which produces superior medicinal herbs capable of curing all diseases.

I shall now speak a verse concerning this:
"Just as the Great Snowy Mountain produces supreme and wondrous medicines that cure all diseases, so too for those who take them..."
Having received this prescription, do not harbor further doubt.
This medicine of wondrous wisdom is born to heal all people from the afflictions of birth, aging, and sickness; it bestows its benefits upon all with impartiality.
"All who consume [this medicine] shall undoubtedly and certainly be cured.

"It is like a person who takes refuge in the new moon, yet does not take refuge in the full moon."

That Tathāgata is born from the Bodhisattva;
whereas Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are born from the Tathāgata, they are not like the Bodhisattva.
Therefore, I shall now speak a verse concerning this:
"Just as these sentient beings take refuge in the new moon, yet do not take refuge in the full moon;
so too is my son, who takes refuge in the Bodhisattva."
They do not turn toward the World-Honored One, for they possess great power of wisdom.
They give birth to the body of a Tathāgata; they are not of the class of śrāvakas, because their wisdom is feeble and inferior. Thus, they take birth by relying upon that Tathāgata.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa: “Kāśyapa,
it is like the mother of all letters, which is fully capable of encompassing all matters such as treatises on meaning.”
In this way, a Bodhisattva who has first resolved their mind is fully able to grasp and encompass the causes of the supreme wisdom of all Buddhas’ transformative practices.
Regarding this, I shall now speak in verse:
"Just as the primary letters of the alphabet, Among both humans and those in the heavens..."
Doctrinal treatises and eloquence are all established on this basis.
So too it is with the Bodhisattva: from the first generation of the bodhicitta, they are fully endowed with the wisdom of the Buddha-ground and all skillful means.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa: "Kāśyapa,
it is like people of the world who would never abandon the bright moon to take refuge in the images of stars."
Thus, there is no one who receives my precepts; having abandoned the Bodhisattvas, they take refuge in the Śrāvakas.
Regarding this, I shall now speak in verse:
"Just as people in the world, Having abandoned the moon..."
Yet to wish to take refuge in the stars—such a thing has never occurred.
It is the same for my disciples; this principle applies likewise:
those who receive my precepts do not take refuge in bodhisattvas.
"And yet they desire to turn toward the Śrāvakas—this matter is most rare.

"It is like a counterfeit lapis lazuli bead; in the world of devas and humans, it is ultimately of no practical use."
