If that true lapis lazuli and that maṇi jewel differ in their essential nature,
yet both serve as vessels for great utility; so too it is with those śrāvakas,
who, though they possess the dhūta practices, [are not equal to the Buddha].
Observing the precepts and extensive learning, as well as all samādhis,
cannot subdue the four māras and enable one to sit upon the bodhi-seat and become a Sugata; this is not the case for the Bodhisattva.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
“For example, when a genuine lapis lazuli maṇi jewel is put to practical use, its value is worth hundreds of thousands of kārṣāpaṇas.”
Kāśyapa! In this way, when the various virtues planted by that bodhisattva are put to use, they are many times greater than those of a hundred thousand kārṣāpaṇas of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
I shall now speak a verse on this matter:
"Just as genuine lapis lazuli And those mani-jewels,
when performing their respective functions, Are worth hundreds of thousands in value."
The *kārsāpaṇa* coin is planted as the root of manifold virtues; its practical application benefits sentient beings far more than those śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
"The number of *kārsāpaṇas* is likewise so.
Then the World-Honored One spoke again:
"Venerable Mahākāśyapa!"
In whatever land the planet Bhauma appears, its head blackened and lying prostrate, it causes calamities to arise in competition within that land, bringing about suffering and distress.
Kāśyapa! If there is a bodhisattva in that land, these various calamities will be swiftly eliminated, and there will be no further suffering or distress.
Therefore, Kāśyapa, the practice of a bodhisattva consists in extensively gathering all roots of goodness for the sake of benefiting sentient beings.

Furthermore, the medicinal wisdom possessed by that bodhisattva circulates throughout the four quarters, healing the diseases of affliction and the like of all sentient beings; it is true and not false.
Kāśyapa replied, "With what medicine does one treat what illness?
[The Buddha said: "Kāśyapa!"
All the maladies of greed, hatred, and delusion possessed by sentient beings arise from conditions.

Through the compassion that is free of conditions (*apratihata-maitrī*), one contemplates all those afflictions and karmas as having appearance but lacking reality; they are fundamentally unborn from the beginning and now likewise devoid of characteristics.
The same applies to the cessation of the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm.
Furthermore, it extinguishes all perversions.
What are these perversions?
That is, the four inversions:
first, because those sentient beings perceive what is impermanent as permanent, one causes them to perceive that all things are impermanent;
second, because they perceive what is suffering as pleasure, one causes them to perceive that all things are suffering.
Third is the conception of self where there is no self, which causes one to perceive that all phenomena are without self;
fourth is the conception of purity where there is impurity, which causes one to perceive that all things are not pure.
Only this nirvāṇa possesses those four virtues.
Furthermore, the four foundations of mindfulness are established so that sentient beings may contemplate the body as having nothing belonging to it, thereby destroying the view of self;
and contemplate feelings as having no feeling to be obtained, thereby destroying that view of self.
One contemplates the mind as having no mind to be found, thereby eliminating the grasping of the view of a self;
one contemplates phenomena as having no phenomena to be found, thereby destroying the grasping of a self in phenomena (*dharmātman*).
By means of the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), regarding the task of cultivation and abandonment, one diligently cultivates what is wholesome and diligently abandons what is unwholesome.

By means of the four bases of psychic power, one accomplishes supernormal powers; by means of the five faculties and five powers, one remedies lack of faith, laziness, forgetfulness, distraction, delusion, and so forth; by means of the seven factors of enlightenment, one remedies all forms of ignorance; and by means of the eightfold noble path, one remedies all faults such as the eightfold wrong path and total lack of knowledge.
Kāśyapa! This is called the teaching of the true medical method. Kāśyapa!
Observe this bodhisattva, who is the foremost among all physicians and healers within Jambudvīpa. Kāśyapa!
All sentient beings in the trichiliocosm, in order to protect their own lives, regard that bodhisattva as they would a king of physicians.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“For those who abide in such wrong views, what medicine should be used for their treatment?
I pray that you will explain this so that they may understand.”

“Kāśyapa! That bodhisattva heals and cures sentient beings not by means of worldly medicines, but by means of the medicine of all supramundane roots of goodness and untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*). He transmits this throughout the four quarters to treat the disease of delusive conceptualization (*parikalpita*) in all those sentient beings; it is true and not false.”
Kāśyapa said: “What is called supramundane wisdom? [The Buddha replied: “Kāśyapa!”

That wisdom arises from the seeds of causes and conditions and is free from all conceptual discrimination; it is without self, without person, without sentient beings, and without life-span. Such wisdom and phenomena are unattached within emptiness.
Kāśyapa! You should seek correctly; let your minds not be terrified, but arouse the mind of diligence.
They seek in this way and abide with their minds in this way.
What is the abiding mind?
What is the non-abiding mind?
Since there are the past, future, and present, in what does it abide?
Kāśyapa! The past has already ceased, the future has not yet arrived, and the present does not abide. Kāśyapa!
Furthermore, this mental phenomenon is neither within, nor without, nor in between.
Kāśyapa! Moreover, this mental phenomenon is free from all marks of form; it is without abiding, without attachment, and is invisible.
“Kāśyapa! All Buddhas of the past are not seen; all Buddhas of the future are not seen; all Buddhas of the present are not seen.
Kāśyapa addressed [the Buddha], saying:
"If all Buddhas of the past, future, and present do not perceive it, how can that mind have various modes of activity?
"Kāśyapa! [The Buddha replied:]
"That mind has no reality; it arises from false conceptualization.
It is like a magical illusion, appearing in various forms through false perception.
Kāśyapa addressed him, saying:
“What is the analogy for that which is false and unreal?
The Buddha said, “Kāśyapa!”

The mind is like a floating bubble, arising and ceasing without abiding; the mind is like the movement of the wind, which cannot be gathered; the mind is like the light of a lamp, produced by the conjunction of causes and conditions; the mind is like empty space, wherein false afflictions arise; the mind is like a flash of lightning, not remaining for even a single kṣaṇa; the mind is like a monkey, grasping at sensory objects; the mind is like a painter, creating all manner of images; the mind is a thought-moment that does not abide, giving rise to all afflictions.
The essence of mental activity is one, for there is no dual functioning of the mind.
The mind is like a king, for it sovereignly conditions all phenomena.
The mind is like an evil friend, for it gives rise to all suffering.
The mind is like the great ocean, for it causes all roots of goodness to drift away and drown.
The mind is like a fisherman, for it conceives the notion of pleasure within suffering.
The mind is like a dream or an illusion, for it falsely calculates a self.
The mind is like a blue fly, for it conceives the notion of purity regarding that which is impure.
The mind is like a malevolent spirit, for it performs all manner of unwholesome deeds.
The mind is like a yakṣa, for it greedily clings to sensory objects and drinks away the vital essence of persons.
The mind is like an enemy, for it constantly seeks out faults;
the mind does not abide in tranquility, for it fluctuates between highs and lows with no fixed course;
the mind is like a mad thief, for it destroys all the wealth of merit and virtue.
The mind is like the eye of a moth, for it constantly craves the color of a lamp’s flame.
The mind is attached to sound, as if craving the sound of a battle drum.
The mind is like a pig or a dog, for it craves fragrant odors within that which is impure.
The mind is like a lowly servant, for it covets the taste of leftovers;
the mind can crave tactile sensations, like a fly clinging to a vessel containing something pungent. Kāśyapa!
The mind cannot be sought; it cannot be obtained through seeking. It did not exist in the past, it does not exist in the future, and it is not found in the present.
If it is unobtainable in the past, future, and present, then the three periods of time are severed.
If the three periods of time are severed, then that does not exist.
If that does not exist, then it does not arise.
If it does not arise, then it is without intrinsic nature.
If that lacks intrinsic nature, there is neither arising nor ceasing.
If there is neither arising nor ceasing, there is also no coming or going.
If there is no coming or going, there is no sovereign master.
If there is no sovereign master, neither provisional nor substantial, this is the nature of the sage.

Kāśyapa! If that nature of the sage exists, there is neither the attainment of precepts nor the absence of precepts; there is neither pure conduct nor defiled conduct; there is neither causal conduct nor resultant conduct; and furthermore, there is no dharma of mind or thought.
If there are no phenomena of mind and consciousness, there is neither karma nor the retribution of karma.
If there is no retribution of karma, there is neither suffering nor pleasure.
If there is neither suffering nor pleasure, that is the nature of the noble one.
If that noble nature has no superior, inferior, or intermediate states, then one must not dwell in or become attached to body, speech, or mind.
Why is this? Because its nature pervades all of space.
"Because it is equal and without discrimination.

The Dharma-transmitting Master, Your Servant Shi Hu, respectfully translates by imperial decree. The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Suppose there is a person skilled in training horses; though the horse is by nature wicked and difficult to subdue, through this person's training, it naturally becomes well-behaved and excellent."

Kāśyapa! A bhikṣu who practices in such a manner is able to maintain the prohibitions and precepts. Although the consciousness of the mind rushes about restlessly and is difficult to subdue, it is tamed and controlled by this bhikṣu; thus, free from anger and the like, he remains as immovable as suchness.
I shall now speak a verse on this matter:
"Just as a horse of evil temperament, When encountered by a skilled trainer,
Is brought under control through various means, And before long becomes well-tamed."
“The bhikṣu who practices in accordance [with the Dharma], who skillfully upholds the prohibitions and precepts,
and who tames the conscious mind, shall cause it to dwell in pure tranquility.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
“Suppose, for example, there is a person who suffers from a goiter in their throat, which destroys their life-force and brings them great suffering.
Kāśyapa, in the same way,
if another person is deeply attached to the notion of a self, they will experience great suffering after this life.”
I shall now speak a verse on this matter:
"Just as a person afflicted with a goiter, Tormented in body and life,
Throughout the day and night, Finds no moment of peace or happiness."
"For sentient beings who are attached to a self, the meaning is likewise so:
seeing things perversely destroys their bodies, and thereafter they give rise to all manner of suffering.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Just as a person whose body is bound may find a skillful means to gain liberation,
so it is, Kāśyapa:
if those sentient beings act in accordance with what is wholesome, they can restrain the monkey-like mind and cause it to be freed from its bonds."
I shall now speak a verse concerning this:
"Just as one who is bound, By employing skillful means,
Can loosen the bonds of body and life, And cause the body to attain mastery."
"The virtuous beings who are in accord, Restraining their mind and consciousness, Cause them to be free from entanglements; The meaning is likewise thus.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
“Suppose, for example, that space is originally vast and empty, yet there are two things capable of covering it.
What are these two things?
They are clouds and mist.”

Kāśyapa! Thus, for one who has gone forth, to seek worldly spells and arts when they are inherently tranquil by nature, and furthermore to accumulate and enjoy robes, alms bowls, and material gains—this constitutes an obscuration.
I shall now speak a verse regarding this:
"Just as clouds and mist Obscure and veil the sky;
so too it is with the bhikṣu who practices the worldly dharmas."
"Practicing incantations and accumulating robes and bowls—
these two obstacles to the practitioner must be avoided by the Bodhisattva.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
“There are two kinds of fetters for these renunciants. What are the two? Kāśyapa!”
First, being bound by gain and offerings; second, being bound by fame and reputation.
Those who have left the household life should each distance themselves from these.
Regarding this, I shall now speak in verse:
"If those who have left the household life are greedily attached to gain and offerings,
as well as to the love of fame— these two heavy fetters also obstruct noble liberation;
one who has left the household life must keep far away from them."
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"There are two kinds of dharmas that extinguish the virtue of one who has gone forth.
What are these two dharmas?"
First, associating with householders; second, harboring resentment toward noble ones.
Regarding this, I shall now speak in verse:
"Associating with householders, And harboring resentment toward noble ones..."
"These two are not the way of the Dharma; they destroy the virtues of one who has gone forth.
A bodhisattva who has left the household life should quickly distance himself from them.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
“There are two kinds of dharmas that serve as defilements for one who has gone forth. What are these two?
First, a mind full of many afflictions; second, abandoning virtuous friends and associating with evil friends.”
I shall now speak a verse on this matter:
"If that renunciant has a mind full of afflictions,
Rejecting and turning away from virtuous friends, And instead drawing near to evil companions."
The Buddha said: "For such a person, I declare that they are a defilement to those who have gone forth.
All members of the bodhisattva assembly should each keep them at a distance.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
“There are two kinds of dharmas that are like standing on a precipice for those who have left the household life. What are these two?
First, slighting the sublime Dharma; second, delighting in the breaking of the precepts.”
I shall now speak a verse regarding this:
"If a renunciant Despises the sublime Dharma And places his trust in those who break the precepts, It is like climbing a perilous cliff."
"Will fall into ruin in an instant.
These two are not the discipline; all sons of the Buddha must distance themselves from those two.
Thus spoke the Buddha to Kāśyapa.
“There are two kinds of dharmas that constitute faults for one who has gone forth. What are these two?
First, seeing the faults of others; second, concealing one’s own faults.”
I shall now speak a verse on this matter:
"If there be one who has gone forth, Who constantly sees the faults of others While concealing his own transgressions— These two are great failings."
"Affliction and harm are as poisonous as fire; the wise must keep far away from them.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"There are two kinds of dharmas that increase the feverish affliction of those who have left the household life."
What are the two kinds?
First, wearing the kashaya while harboring impure thoughts; second, relying on one's own virtue of precepts to revile those of improper conduct.
Regarding this, I shall now speak in verse:
"Though one may wear the kāṣāya, if their mental conduct is impure;
or if, despite possessing the virtue of precepts in body, they employ harsh speech;
or if they seek to suppress those who do not practice—these two must be avoided."
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"There are two kinds of dharmas that heal the illnesses of those who have gone forth.
What are these two dharmas?"
First, those who practice the Mahāyāna attain certainty of mind; second, they ensure that the Buddha-dharma is not interrupted for all sentient beings.
Now, regarding this, I shall speak in verse:
"If there be one who has gone forth And practices that Mahāyāna conduct..."
"One whose mind is always resolute and who does not sever the Buddha-dharma—
these two kinds of renunciants, the Buddha says, are called 'free from illness.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"There are two kinds of dharmas that constitute chronic illnesses for those who have gone forth. What are the two?
First, committing a grave offense (āpatti) of pārājika; second, being unable to disclose and repent of it."
I shall now speak a verse concerning this matter:
“The assembly of renunciant bhikṣus, having committed an āpatti, Fails to repent and extinguish their transgression;
Deluded and ignorant, they do not revere the precepts.”
"Realizing [the truth] moment by moment, this evil shall long remain as a disease.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"There are those who are śramaṇas only in name."
Kāśyapa replied: "In what way is a śramaṇa designated by the name 'śramaṇa'?
[The Buddha said: "Kāśyapa!"
There are four kinds of śramaṇas. What are the four?
First, the śramaṇa who practices the outward appearance; second, the śramaṇa who secretly practices deceit; third, the śramaṇa who seeks fame and praise; and fourth, the śramaṇa of true practice.
“Kāśyapa, these are the four kinds of śramaṇas. Kāśyapa replied:
“What is meant by a śramaṇa who merely conforms to the outward appearance? Kāśyapa!

Such a śramaṇa, though he has shaved off his hair and beard, dons the Buddha’s kāṣāya robe, and maintains a begging bowl—thus being fully endowed with the outward marks—yet his body is impure, his speech is impure, and his mind is impure. He is not self-subdued; he is coarse, evil, and unwholesome. He greedily craves wealth and profit, his livelihood is impure, and he incurs the transgression of violating the precepts.”
“Kāśyapa! This is called the śramaṇa who practices the signs of form.
Kāśyapa addressed him, saying:
"What is meant by a śramaṇa who secretly practices deceit? Kāśyapa!

Such a śramaṇa, though he knows his conduct and possesses outward decorum, eats coarse and unwholesome food; he feigns joy and feigns delight, constantly engaging in falsehood while walking, standing, sitting, or lying down. Furthermore, he does not associate with the four noble lineages of householders or renunciants; he feigns silence and remains speechless to deceive and mislead sentient beings. His mind lacks purity and lacks self-mastery, and he never rests in mindfulness, but instead engages in false conjecture."

They cling to the marks of self and person; when encountering the dharma of emptiness, they give rise to fear as if climbing a perilous precipice, and when seeing a bhikṣu who skillfully discourses on emptiness, they regard him as an enemy.
“Kāśyapa! This is what is called a ‘secretly practicing, deceitful śramaṇa.
Kāśyapa addressed [the Buddha], saying:
"What is meant by a śramaṇa who seeks fame, renown, and praise?

"Kāśyapa! Such a śramaṇa falsely practices the observance of precepts for the sake of seeking fame, renown, and praise; he deludes others and, relying on his extensive learning, flaunts it to demand their praise."

Whether dwelling in the mountains and wilds or staying amidst the forests, they falsely manifest few desires and lack of greed, and feign the practice of pure conduct; yet within their hearts, they possess no renunciation of desire, no tranquility, no cessation of thought, and no realization of Bodhi. They are neither śramaṇas nor brāhmaṇas, nor do they seek nirvāṇa, but rather seek praise and fame.
“Kāśyapa, this is called the śramaṇa who seeks fame, renown, and praise.
Kāśyapa addressed [the Buddha], saying:
“What is meant by a śramaṇa who practices according to reality? “Kāśyapa!

Such a śramaṇa does not engage in external affairs for the sake of his body or life, nor does he speak of fame, reputation, profit, or sustenance; he practices only emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.”

Having heard all dharmas, one correctly contemplates the reality-limit of nirvāṇa, constantly cultivates the pure conduct (brahmacarya) without seeking worldly retribution, and does not deliberate upon the matters of joy and pleasure within the triple world. One perceives only the emptiness of nature and does not grasp at phenomenal dharmas, nor does one discuss the self, persons, sentient beings, life-span, or the *pudgala*.

Seeing the stage of the True Dharma, one is free from all delusions; on the path of liberation, one severs all afflictions and realizes that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is pure. Being unattached to either the internal or the external, with neither accumulation nor dispersion, one clearly and thoroughly penetrates that Dharmakāya Tathāgata.

He is free from the grasping of views and does not engage in discursive speech; his physical body is detached from desire, and he perceives neither the marks of form nor the activities of the three karmas, nor does he cling to the assembly of ordinary beings or sages.

All phenomena are non-existent; severed from all conceptual discrimination, their intrinsic nature is immovable. One neither attains saṃsāra nor nirvāṇa; there is neither bondage nor liberation, neither coming nor going. Thus one knows that all phenomena are quiescent and profoundly still.
Kāśyapa! This is called a śramaṇa of true practice who performs corresponding conduct, not for the sake of seeking fame.
Regarding this, I shall now speak in verse:
"All actions of body, speech, and mind— The three karmas are not pure;
Craving is unsubdued, And coarse conduct is not restrained.
Shaven-headed and clad in the three robes, Holding the alms-bowl,"
The Buddha has said that these śramaṇas constantly practice regarding the marks of physical form.
Although they rely on such practices, they are deceptive and unreal;
they falsely manifest the four dignified demeanors to appear as if they were noble ones.
Dwelling far from places of harmony, Constantly consuming coarse and unwholesome food,
Lacking those pure practices, They secretly engage in deceit.
Or, seeking fame for themselves, They insist that others offer them praise.
Falsely cultivating precepts and meditative concentration, they display the practice of dhūta austerities.
With their inner minds unsubdued, they deceive those who offer gifts of faith;
they do not practice the goodness of detachment from desire, nor do they still the攀緣 (pān-yuán, clinging to conditions).
Seeing that the characteristics of dharmas are empty, they are terrified as if climbing a perilous mountain;
though they may dwell among mountains and wilds, they lack the intent for what is real.
The Buddha says these śramaṇas do so for the sake of seeking fame and reputation.
If one is a true practitioner, they do not, for the sake of body or life,
falsely seek fame, profit, or sustenance; nor do they seek pleasure,
but practice only for right liberation, rescuing and delivering all from the evil realms.
Though knowing that profound dharmas are empty, one does not attain tranquility, nor is there non-tranquility;
one does not dwell in nirvana, nor does one attain saṃsāra; one does not cling to the noble ones.
They do not abandon ordinary beings;
originally they have nowhere from which they come, and now they have nowhere to which they go—all phenomena are tranquil.
Of such a person, the Buddha says: "This is called one who practices in accordance with reality."
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
“It is like a poor man who has no wealth or profit in his house, yet he makes this declaration to the multitude, saying:
‘Within my house there is a great storehouse, filled to overflowing with treasures.’”
"Kāśyapa! What do you think?
Is what this poor man says true?"
Kāśyapa replied, “No, World-Honored One.”
The Buddha said, “Kāśyapa, it is just so.”
Those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas themselves possess no virtue of precepts, yet they speak these words:
"I am endowed with great virtuous karma.
These words are untrue; such a matter is difficult to believe.
I shall now speak a verse concerning this matter:
"Just as a poor man might say, 'I possess a storehouse filled with the seven kinds of precious treasures,' yet his words do not correspond to reality."
"Śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas are likewise false and deceptive;
their three karmas are not pure, yet they claim themselves to be endowed with the virtue of the precepts.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
“Suppose, for example, there is a person who enters deep water but is not focused; heedlessly playing in the water, he does not realize he is drowning.
Kāśyapa, it is just the same.”

These śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, though possessing great knowledge and delighting in the Dharma, enter the great ocean of the Dharma yet cannot restrain their minds; being fond of practicing greed, hatred, and delusion, they are led by the afflictions of craving into the evil realms.
I shall now speak a verse regarding this matter:
"Just as a person playing in the water, Who enters into the midst of a great flood,
Fails to exercise self-control over his mind, And is drowned by the water, losing his life."
“Śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who greedily enter the great ocean of the Dharma,
yet act wantonly under the influence of greed, hatred, and delusion, will sink and fall into the evil destinies.
Thus the Buddha told Kāśyapa:

“Suppose, for example, a physician compiles and prepares medicinal decoctions, intending to take them to the four quarters to treat various ailments, yet suddenly falls ill himself and is unable to cure his own condition. Kāśyapa!
In this way, if that bhikṣu has cultivated much learning and desires to transform sentient beings, yet suddenly afflictions arise within him and he is unable to subdue them.
I shall now speak a verse on this matter:
"Just as a skilled physician, having prepared various decoctions and medicines,
carries them to the four quarters to treat the illnesses of the multitude of beings."
When one suddenly falls ill, one cannot treat the malady oneself;
so it is with the bhikṣu: though he has cultivated much learning and desires to practice the guidance of others, when afflictions suddenly arise within himself, [he is unable to cure them].
"Unable to properly restrain [the mind], one undergoes suffering in vain.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"It is like a person who has a grave illness; though they take the finest and most renowned medicines, they cannot avoid meeting their end."
Kāśyapa! It is just so:
if those sentient beings possess the disease of afflictions, even if they desire much learning and practice, they cannot avoid falling into ruin.
Regarding this, I shall now speak a verse:
"Just as a gravely ill person, suffering for a long time without recovery,
may take excellent medicine yet ultimately cannot escape impermanence;
so it is with sentient beings, who are constantly afflicted by the disease of the defilements."
"Even if one provides music and cultivates extensive learning, one cannot avoid falling into ruin.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"It is like a maṇi jewel that has fallen into impurity; because its substance has been defiled by contact, it is unfit for use."
Kāśyapa! In this way, even if a bhikṣu is possessed of great learning, if he falls into impure gain and offerings, gods and humans will not feel reverence or affection for him.
I shall now speak a verse regarding this:
"Just as a mani jewel, having fallen into impurity,
becomes defiled by contact with it and is no longer fit for use."
So it is with a bhikṣu: though he may possess great learning,
if he falls into impurity amidst fame and gain,
neither the devas nor the people will feel love or respect for him.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
“Suppose, for example, there were a person who suddenly passed away, yet his head and face were adorned with a golden crown and flower garlands.
Kāśyapa, in the same way, if a bhikṣu has utterly destroyed the precepts, what benefit is there in adorning his body with the kāṣāya robe?”
I shall now speak a verse regarding this matter:
"Just as when a person has died, one might adorn their corpse with beautiful flower garlands and crowns of gold and jewels;
yet, even though it is thus decorated, the body will not rise up again."
Such a person has no purpose;
though they wear the saṃghāṭī robe upon a body of broken precepts,
and assume a majestic deportment through outward adornment, in the end there is no benefit.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:

"Suppose there is a person who has bathed until completely clean, who anoints his body, head, topknot, and fingernails with fragrant oil, and who, wearing white garments and a garland of *campaka* flowers, is a member of a noble family."
Kāśyapa! It is thus:
if a bhikṣu is learned and wise, clad in the Dharma robes with full observance of the proper deportment, he is a disciple of the Buddha.
Regarding this, I shall now speak a verse:
"Just as people in the world, having bathed until their bodies are pure,
anointing themselves with fine fragrant oils, adorning their heads with flower garlands,
and wearing white garments, are called sons of noble lineage."
The bhikṣu is likewise: learned and endowed with dhāraṇī, his ethical virtue ever pure;
clad in the dharma-robe and complete in dignified appearance—this one is called a true son of the Buddha.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"There are four kinds of precept-breaking bhikṣus who are like reflections of those who uphold the precepts.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“What are the four kinds of breaking the precepts? “Kāśyapa,

there is a bhikṣu who fully receives and upholds the Prātimokṣa precepts, is well-versed in the prohibitions and the Vinaya, feels deep dread and fear regarding even minor offenses, always relies upon the training rules, maintains purity in the recitation of the precepts, is complete in his actions of body, speech, and mind without transgression, and his livelihood is free from wrong means.”
This entails a fault. Why is this so?
Because by clinging to one's own efficacy, one falls into the grasping of rules and rituals (śīlavrataparāmarśa).
Kāśyapa! This is the first analogy for breaking the precepts as a semblance of upholding them.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa!
There was a bhikṣu who was well-versed in the prohibitions and the Vinaya, constantly maintaining his observance of the precepts and secretly employing the three karmas.
Yet he possessed the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi), for he did not relinquish his clinging attachments. Kāśyapa!
This is the second illustration of breaking the precepts as a semblance of upholding them.

"Furthermore, Kāśyapa, there is a bhikṣu who constantly practices loving-kindness and compassion for sentient beings, being fully endowed with kindness and charity; yet he harbors malice toward another bhikṣu."
Upon hearing that all phenomena are unarisen, their minds are struck with fear and alarm.
Kāśyapa, this is the third analogy for one who breaks the precepts yet maintains the semblance of upholding them.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa,
there may be a bhikṣu who practices those twelve dhūta ascetic virtues fully and without deficiency;
yet he harbors a sense of self and dwells attached to the marks of a self and a person."
Kāśyapa! This is the fourth analogy for one who breaks the precepts yet bears the semblance of upholding them. Kāśyapa!

These four types of breaking the precepts are metaphors for the semblance of upholding the precepts. "Furthermore, Kāśyapa, if one speaks of these precepts, there is no person, no self, no sentient being, and no life-span;

there is neither practice nor non-practice, neither action nor non-action; they are neither transgressions nor non-transgressions; they have no name and no form, yet are not without name and form; they have no marks, yet are not without marks; they have no cessation of thought, yet are not without cessation of thought; they have no grasping and no relinquishing, yet are not without grasping and relinquishing; they are neither receiving nor not receiving; they have no consciousness and no mind, yet are not without consciousness and mind; they have neither the mundane nor the supramundane; they have no place of abiding, yet are not without abiding; there is no self-upholding of the precepts and no other-upholding of the precepts."
Within this precept, one is free from all slander, confusion, and attachment.
Kāśyapa! This is called the noble, untainted right precept, which remains far removed from all dwelling places within the three realms.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"The undefiled precepts one upholds Do not dwell upon the marks of self or person.
There is neither transgression nor upholding; Neither bondage nor liberation."
Subtle, profound, and virtuous, It is far removed from doubt and confusion.
Kāśyapa, these characteristics of the precepts Are the true teaching of the Tathāgata.
Those who uphold this stainless morality Within that world...
Not for the sake of one's own life, but to universally deliver all sentient beings,
so that they may together enter the limit of True Suchness (Tathatā).
Kāśyapa, these characteristics of the precepts are the true teaching of the Tathāgata.
"The stainless precepts he upholds, among those beings and within himself, are neither defiled nor pure; they are neither dark nor bright;
there is neither gain nor loss; he does not abide on this shore."
Not reaching the further shore, nor remaining in the middle of the stream;
bound and liberated are equal, abiding nowhere like space—
neither with marks nor without marks.
Kāśyapa, these characteristics of the precepts were spoken truly by the Tathāgata:
"One who upholds the stainless precepts does not cling to name-and-form, nor does he dwell in meditative absorption; with a perpetually pure and sublime mind,"
Free from the marks of self, existence,
and non-existence; far removed from observance and violation, there is neither precept nor non-precept,
neither concentration nor distraction.
When wisdom observes the non-duality of subject and object, this precept is pure and subtle;
abiding in samādhi, one gives rise to contemplation from within samādhi,
and wisdom becomes naturally purified— this is called the fulfillment of the precepts.
The Sūtra on the Great Dharma Accumulation as Asked by Mahākāśyapa, Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Four.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master Śīladharma, Dharma Master and Subject Shi Hu, who holds the rank of Chao-san Dafu and Acting Assistant Director of the Court of State Ceremonial, by Imperial Decree.

At that time, when the World-Honored One spoke this verse-dharma, eight hundred bhikṣus attained the exhaustion of outflows and the liberation of mind through the understanding of the Dharma; three billion people were distanced from dust and freed from defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.

Five hundred bhikṣus who had attained samādhi, upon hearing this profound and subtle Dharma of the precepts—which is difficult to understand and difficult to enter—did not believe it nor did they study it; they rose from their seats and quickly departed from the Buddha’s assembly.
At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa addressed the Blessed One, saying:

"These five hundred bhikṣus have attained samādhi; why is it that upon hearing this most profound Dharma—which is difficult to understand and difficult to enter—they do not believe or study it, but instead rise from their seats and withdraw immediately?"
The Buddha said, “Kāśyapa!

Those five hundred bhikṣus have not yet eliminated their views; having heard this stainless and pure Dharma of the precepts, they find it difficult to understand and difficult to enter. Their minds are filled with alarm and fear, which is why they do not believe or practice it.”

Kāśyapa! This dharma of the verses on the precepts is profoundly deep and subtle; the enlightenment of the three Buddhas all issues from it, yet those sinful companions cannot enter into this wondrous goodness of liberation.
Furthermore, he addressed them, saying: "Kāśyapa!
Those five hundred bhikṣus are heterodox śrāvakas within the teaching of the Tathāgata."
Thus it is, Kāśyapa!

Because they cling to and seek a single dharma according to their own original intentions regarding the Tathāgata, if they hear even one dharma and accept it with firm faith, yet find that the teaching upon which they rely for study and practice—such as these verses—is profound and subtle, they consequently become startled and terrified.
Again he said: "Kāśyapa!

That bhikṣu’s intention was to seek out a single dharma from the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, and to practice with a mind thus resolved; yet after his life ended, he sought rebirth in the Tuṣita Heaven. It was for such a purpose that he sought to go forth in the Buddha's teaching."

Kāśyapa! These five hundred bhikṣus have not yet abandoned the view of a self-existent body; having heard this profound Dharma, they give rise to alarm and fear, and neither believe nor study it. Upon the end of their lives, these individuals will certainly fall into the evil destinies.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Subhūti, saying:
"Go to where the five hundred bhikṣus are and instruct them with skillful means."
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One, when they hear such teachings and instructions as these, they do not believe them nor put them into practice.
My own wisdom is slight and my learning is meager; how could I transform them?”

At that time, five hundred bhikṣus were already on the road. Then the World-Honored One, by means of his supernatural power, manifested two bhikṣus who met the five hundred bhikṣus halfway along the road and asked them:
"Venerable ones!..."
"Where do you wish to go?
The bhikṣus replied, "We now wish to go to the forest; there, in that state of tranquility, we shall dwell, attaining the bliss of meditative concentration for ourselves."
The transformed bhikṣu asked,
"What do you think of dwelling in the forest wilds? Those bhikṣus then replied:

“The Dharma taught by the Blessed One is something we have never heard before; having now heard it, it is difficult to understand and difficult to enter. Our minds are struck with fear and alarm, and we cannot believe or study it. Therefore, we prefer to return to the forest and wilderness to dwell securely in meditative concentration and attain peace.”
The transformed bhikṣu said:
"Venerable ones!

The Dharma taught by the World-Honored One is difficult to understand; having conceived fear and dread, they do not believe, study, or practice it, but instead retreat to the forest and take meditative concentration to be nirvāṇa—this is what they cling to, which you do not know."
Venerable sir!
The Dharma of the śramaṇa is not something to be debated or cross-examined.
Now, I ask you, venerable sir!
What is called the dharma of nirvāṇa?
If one were to attain nirvāṇa within one's own body, then one would have obtained a *pudgala*, a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span; how then could there be nirvāṇa?
"Indeed, the dharma of nirvāṇa is neither characterized by marks nor devoid of marks. That bhikṣu asked:
"If nirvāṇa is thus, how is it realized?"
The transformed bhikṣu said:
"It is the dharma that eradicates greed, hatred, and delusion. That bhikṣu said:
"How are the phenomena of greed, hatred, and delusion to be abandoned?

The manifested bhikṣu replied, "The phenomena of greed, hatred, and delusion are neither within, nor without, nor in between; they are fundamentally unarisen from the beginning and are likewise not subject to cessation now."
The transformed bhikṣu said:
"Venerable sir!
You must neither grasp nor doubt."
Venerable sir, if one neither clings nor doubts, being neither protected nor unprotected, neither delighted nor undelighted—that, they say, is Nirvana.
Venerable sir!

This mark of pure precepts is neither born nor extinguished; it arises from samādhi, arises from wisdom, arises from liberation, and arises from the knowledge and vision of liberation. It is free from existence and free from non-existence; it is neither a mark nor the absence of a mark.
Venerable One!
Such characteristics of precepts are themselves true nirvāṇa.
In such nirvāṇa, there is no liberation to be attained and no afflictions to be abandoned.
"Venerable One!
If you seek parinirvāṇa through conceptualization and mental ideation, this is the attainment of delusive thought, not nirvāṇa.
If one gives rise to ideation within ideation, it is not nirvāṇa; one is thereby bound and fettered by ideation."
"In this way, if one extinguishes sensation and perception, one attains the true *samāpatti*.
Venerable One!
For a practitioner who acts thus, there is nothing superior."

At that time, while the emanated being was preaching this True Dharma, those five hundred bhikṣus, having heard this teaching, were freed from outflows, their minds attained liberation, and they achieved deliverance of heart.
Thus, those five hundred bhikṣus again went to where the Buddha was; having arrived, they prostrated with their heads at his feet, circumambulated him three times, and sat down to one side.
At that time, the Elder Subhūti rose from his seat and asked those bhikṣus:
"Venerable sirs!..."
"Where have you been? From where do you come now? He replied:
"It was not originally going anywhere, and now it does not come.
The Elder Subhūti then asked the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!"
"What is the meaning of this Dharma that has been taught?
The Buddha said:
"It is without arising and without cessation."
Subhūti said: "Venerable ones, how do you hear the Dharma?
Those bhikṣus replied:
"There is neither bondage nor liberation. Subhūti said,
"Who has transformed you?"
The bhikṣu replied, “There is neither body nor mind. Subhūti said:
"How do you practice? Those bhikṣus replied,
"There is neither the cessation of ignorance nor the arising of ignorance."
Subhūti said: "In what way are you a śrāvaka? That bhikṣu replied:
"One shall neither become a śrāvaka nor attain buddhahood.
Subhūti asked: "What, then, is your brahmacarya?"
That bhikṣu said, “I do not dwell in the three realms. Subhūti said:
"At what time will you enter parinirvāṇa?
That bhikṣu replied,
"When the Tathāgata enters parinirvāṇa, I shall enter parinirvāṇa."
Subhūti said: "You have already accomplished what was to be done.
Those bhikṣus replied:
"Having fully understood [the notions of] self and person. Subhūti said:
"Your afflictions have been exhausted."
The bhikṣu said: "All dharmas are also exhausted. Subhūti said:
"You have skillfully defeated the Māra King.
Those bhikṣus replied,
"Since even the aggregate-body cannot be found, how can there be a defeat of the Māra King?"
Subhūti asked, "Do you know your teacher? That bhikṣu replied:
"It is neither body, nor speech, nor mind.
Subhūti said, "You have attained the ground of supreme purity."
The bhikṣu said: "There is neither grasping nor relinquishing. Subhūti said:
"You have emerged from saṃsāra and now reached the other shore.
That bhikṣu replied,
"I have neither reached the other shore, nor do I obtain saṃsāra."
Subhūti said: "Do you believe in the stages of excellence? That bhikṣu replied:
"All attachments are liberated. Subhūti said: "Where will you go?"
The bhikṣu said: "The Tathāgata has gone where he goes.
The transformed bhikṣu said:
“Venerable One! Subhūti, you must let him go.

When this Dharma was spoken, eight hundred bhikṣus within the assembly gave rise to the aspiration for the state of a śrāvaka and attained liberation of mind; thirty-two billion sentient beings became free from dust and removed from defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.
At that time, there was in the assembly a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Samantaprabha, who rose from his seat, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"How should all bodhisattvas train in this sublime Dharma of the Great Ratnakūṭa?
How should they abide?
The Buddha replied:

“Good sons! Regarding the true Dharma and authentic precepts that have been taught, you should receive and uphold them by abiding in this manner; through this true Dharma, you shall attain great and wholesome benefit.”
Good son! It is like a person who, wishing to cross a deep and wide great river, boards a boat made of earth. Good son!
"What do you think?
By what means could that person, traveling upon this earthen boat, quickly reach the other shore?
Pūrvāloka replied:
“World-Honored One!
It must require great power of spirit, courage, and diligent effort to reach the other shore.
The Buddha said:
“Samantaprabha! For what reason must you exert such diligent effort?
“World-Honored One!”
“The current of that river is deep and broad, causing one to feel anxiety and fear; if one does not exert diligent effort, one will surely sink and drown.
The Buddha told Bodhisattva Samantaprabhāsa: “It is so.

If bodhisattvas practice and study the True Dharma, wishing to cross the great river of the four flows of birth and death, they must give rise to the power of courageous and vigorous diligence to penetrate the Buddha-dharma. If they do not diligently practice and study, they will certainly fall back and regress.”
Furthermore, reflect thus: this body is without strength, impermanent, and subject to rapid decay; how can one cross over the vast expanse of the four floods?
Those sentient beings constantly dwell on this shore; you must now take up the great ship of the sublime Dharma to transport all sentient beings across the river of saṃsāra to the shore of bodhi.
The Bodhisattva Samantaprabha again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how does a bodhisattva receive and uphold the great ship of the sublime Dharma?”
“Good son! All acts of giving, upholding the precepts, patience, and loving-kindness accumulate boundless merit; one should give rise to a mind of equanimity to adorn all sentient beings.”

He does not forget the excellence of the seven factors of enlightenment; he diligently upholds them with a mind of firm resolve. Through skillful means, he deeply penetrates the true nature of reality; through great compassion, he extracts the suffering of sentient beings; through the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), he protects all living beings; through the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), he benefits sentient beings; through the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), he constantly reflects within himself; through the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), he diligently abandons what is unwholesome and cultivates what is wholesome; through the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), he manifests supernormal powers; through the five faculties (*indriya*), he causes various virtues to arise; through the five powers (*bala*), he remains firm and non-regressive; through the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*), he stays far removed from the enmity of Māra and does not dwell in deviant paths; and regarding *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, he is signless and unattached.

The Bodhisattva causes this vast practice of the Dharma to be heard throughout the ten directions, enabling all sentient beings to board the great ship of the subtle and sublime True Dharma. Thus they cross over the great river of the four currents of birth and death, reaching the peaceful and blissful shore of Nirvana, where they attain fearlessness and are forever free from all views.

"Good sons! You should know that such bodhisattvas, by means of the great ship of the sublime Dharma, transport all sentient beings across the great river of the four currents for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas without ever becoming weary or exhausted."
"You should uphold it in this way and abide in this way. The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Universal Radiance:

"Now, quickly employ true skillful means and give rise to great compassion, causing the minds and intentions of all sentient beings to be pure and filled with courageous diligence. Cause them to plant various roots of goodness so that they may never regress; always delight in leaving the household life and hearing the Dharma without weariness; plant the foundations of myriad virtues and seek the supreme path; perfect wisdom and maintain tranquility of body and mind; dwell peacefully in forests and wilds, remaining far removed from evil friends; clearly comprehend and penetrate the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*); practice correct skillful means; and regarding the two truths—the ultimate and the conventional—realize that principle and phenomena are non-dual, equal, and one, thereby stilling all deluded thoughts."
“Good son! A bodhisattva, for the sake of all sentient beings, should uphold [the Dharma] in this way and should abide in this way.
At that time, having heard this teaching, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This Great Jewel Heap of the True Dharma is taught for those who seek the Mahāyāna; it has never existed before.
World-Honored One!”

If a son or daughter of good family were to receive, uphold, explain, and expound even a single phrase or a single verse of this sublime Dharma of the Great Ratnakūṭa, what would be the nature of the merit thereby obtained?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
“It should be understood in this way:

if there are sons or daughters of good family who, regarding this Great Ratnakūṭa True Dharma, receive, uphold, and recite even a single phrase or a single verse, the merit they thereby obtain is as follows.”

"Good son! Suppose there were a person who, with the seven treasures filling worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, made offerings to Tathāgatas equal in number to the sands of the Ganges; and for each and every Tathāgata, he separately bestowed as an offering worlds filled with the seven treasures, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; furthermore, for each and every Tathāgata, he constructed Buddhist temples and monasteries, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; and for each and every Tathāgata, there was an immeasurable assembly of śrāvakas, whom he served with all manner of articles of pleasure for a period of one kalpa as numerous as the sands of the Ganges."
Furthermore, after those Tathāgatas and their śrāvaka disciples have entered nirvāṇa, one shall again erect stūpas made of the seven precious gems for each of them.
Son of good family, such merit is immeasurable and boundless.

It is not as meritorious as for someone to receive, uphold, explain, or expound even a single sentence or a single verse of this *Ratnakūṭa* True Dharma; the merit of the latter surpasses that of the former.

Furthermore, if someone explains this sutra for their parents, those people will not fall into the evil realms at the end of their lives, and their mother’s future rebirth will be transformed into that of a male.
The Buddha said:

"Wherever this Great Ratnakūṭa Sūtra is written down, upheld, recited, read, or explained, all the worlds—including devas, humans, and asuras—will revere and make offerings to that place as they would to a stupa or temple of the Buddha."
If there is a Dharma master who, upon hearing this *Ratnakūṭa* Sūtra of the True Dharma, gives rise to a heart of reverence and receives, maintains, reads, recites, copies, and makes offerings to it;

and if there are good sons or good daughters who, toward that Dharma master, provide offerings, respect, honor, prostrations, and praise as they would to the Buddha—those persons shall receive a prophecy from the Buddha in their present life that they will attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and at the time of their death, they shall behold the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, that Dharma master also attains ten kinds of purity of bodily action. What are these ten?
First, at the time of death, he does not undergo various sufferings.
Second, his visual consciousness is clear and lucid, such that he does not perceive evil signs;
third, his arms and hands are stable and steady, such that he does not reach out to grasp at empty space;
fourth, his feet are secure and composed, such that he does not trample upon anything.
Fifth, they do not suffer the leakage of feces or urine;
sixth, their bodies and sense organs do not emit foul odors;
seventh, their abdomens and intestines remain intact and do not become distended.
Eighth, his tongue is long and broad, neither curled nor retracted;
ninth, his eyes are dignified and not unseemly;
tenth, although his body has entered parinirvāṇa, its form and color remain as if alive.
Thus one attains these ten kinds of purity of bodily action.
Furthermore, there are ten kinds of purity of verbal action. What are the ten?
First, his voice is beautiful;
second, what he says is kind and compassionate;
third, his speech is sublime and exquisite.
Fourth, they utter words of loving-kindness;
fifth, their speech is gentle and supple;
sixth, what they say is truthful and sincere.
Seventh, one first speaks words of greeting;
eighth, one speaks with a voice worthy of being heard and accepted;
ninth, one is loved and delighted by devas and humans.
Tenth, as the Buddha has said:
"These ten kinds of verbal karma are pure.
Furthermore, there are ten kinds of mental karma that are pure."
What are the ten?
First, the mind is free from anger;
second, one does not give rise to envy.
Third, not relying on oneself;
fourth, being free from resentment and affliction;
fifth, being devoid of faults.
Sixth, the absence of perverted perceptions;
seventh, the absence of inferior perceptions;
eighth, the absence of perceptions of transgressing the precepts.
Ninth, with right intention and focused mind, one contemplates the Buddha-fields;
tenth, being far removed from the notions of self and person, one attains samādhi and accomplishes all the teachings of the Buddhas.
In this way, one attains the ten kinds of purity of mental action.
I shall now speak a verse on this matter:
"At the time of death, one does not undergo suffering, Nor does one behold various evil omens;
The hands do not clutch at empty space, And the feet have no more kicking or trampling."
The bodily orifices are perfectly sealed without leakage; the sense organ of the body is free from foul odors;
the abdomen is not distended; the tongue is crimson and neither crooked nor shriveled;
the eyes remain dignified and steady; and at the end of life, the countenance does not change.
Such are the ten aspects of the body, The marks of merit, goodness, and purity.
His speech and voice become exquisite; The words he utters are kind and benevolent.
What he says is extraordinary and sublime; When he speaks, people love and delight in it.
Furthermore, there is a voice that is gentle and supple; what it says is truthful and sincere.
It is skillful in inquiry and capable of being heard and accepted by others;
even the hosts of devas and nāgas revere it, for its pure resonance is like the speech of a Buddha.
Thus, through these ten kinds of verbal conduct, one attains purity of speech.
Even if the mind is prone to anger, jealousy shall not arise;
lacking any self-reliance, resentment and affliction will likewise be eliminated of their own accord.
Having attained freedom from all faults, may inverted perceptions not arise;
do not engage in base actions, and let not the prohibitive precepts be impaired.
With right intention, maintain focused mindfulness, and remain far removed from the notions of self and person.
Furthermore, one attains samādhi and penetrates all Buddha-dharmas;
these ten aspects of the mind are the characteristics of the purity of mental karma.
The Buddha told Mahākāśyapa:

“Good sons and good daughters, you should all offer incense, flowers, music, silken canopies, banners, pennants, food, drink, clothing, and all manner of articles of pleasure to this Great Jewel Accumulation True Dharma; with a sincere heart, take refuge in it, receive and uphold it, and recite it.”
Why is this so? Kāśyapa! All these Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas have emerged from this; therefore, one should honor it with the most supreme offerings.

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa received it with single-minded devotion; the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, as well as the bhikṣus, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, and the entire great assembly, were all filled with great joy, and they faithfully accepted and practiced it.
The Sutra on the Great Dharma Accumulation as Asked by Mahākāśyapa, Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Five.
